entries.title: Suspect threw flaming 'Molotov cocktail' before attempted stabbing at UIC Student Center, feds say
entries.summary: <p>A University of Illinois Chicago student has been charged in federal court with possessing a "Molotov cocktail" destructive device on campus, according to court documents.</p><p>The student, identified as 20-year-old Pugazhan Tamizhsami Sathyamurthy, was charged with possessing an unregistered destructive device, according to a criminal complaint. The charge is punishable by up to ten years in federal prison. </p><p>On the afternoon of Nov. 4, Sathyamurthy was on the second floor of the school's Student Center East, 750 S. Halsted St., when he allegedly threw the device while it was on fire toward another individual, according to a criminal complaint. </p><p>After the device hit the floor and shattered, the flame went out. Sathyamurthy then brandished a knife and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/11/04/uic-student-arrested-student-center-evacuated-after-attempted-stabbing-on-campus" target="_blank" >attempted to stab a student</a> before the student escaped, officials said. </p><p>Sathyamurthy was arrested by UIC police officers and a search of his backpack revealed two devices similar to the one Sathyamurthy is accused of throwing in the student center, the complaint states.</p><p>Sathyamurthy was taken into federal custody Monday morning and was expected to appear in federal court later that day before U.S. Magistrate Judge Young B. Kim. The outcome of that hearing could not be confirmed Monday evening.</p>

entries.title: Mike Clark's statewide preseason Super 25 girls basketball rankings
entries.summary: <p>A lot of coaches don't like to broadcast their goals, but Nazareth's Ed Stritzel isn't one of them.</p><p>The Roadrunners want to be the first team to repeat as Class 4A girls basketball state champ since Geneva won back-to-back in 2017-18.</p><p>"It kind of makes sense to us," Stritzel said, "Only one team gets to win it and if you don't, you're disappointed."</p><p>Nazareth had one of the most dominant title-game performances in state history last March, beating runner-up Loyola 55-23.</p><p>Two starters graduated, including current BYU freshman Stella Sakalas. But there's a nice mix of returners from last year's 35-3 team and some incoming talent for the top-ranked Roadrunners.</p><p>"If we jell, we're going to be a tough out," Stritzel said.</p><p>Here's a look at the Super 25 preseason rankings, which for the first time covers the entire state:</p><h3>No. 1 Nazareth</h3><p>Northwestern commit Sophia Towne will shoulder more of the scoring load with Sakalas gone, while Mia Gage is one of the state's elite sophomores and Samantha Austin is a three-year starter. Mollie Moore, the first player off the bench the past two seasons, steps into a starting role along with 6-1 sophomore Hillary Whorlow.</p><p>Two freshmen who already have Division I interest, Ainslie Haunty and Addison Brown, join the mix.</p><h3>No. 2 Belleville East</h3><p>The Lancers pulled off a rare feat last season, finishing third in 4A without a senior — and only one junior — in the starting lineup. Junior point guard Hailey Gray, who picked up her first Division I offer from Chicago State over the summer, sets the tone for East, which will play at Nazareth on Dec. 5 in an early-season showdown.</p><h3>No. 3 Evanston</h3><p>This is a team on the rise. Junior guard Charity Bryant averaged 23.0 points, 7.4 rebounds and 3.1 steals last season en route to earning Central Suburban League Player of the Year honors. Senior guard Payton King (12.7 ppg) is an Oakland commit and sophomore forward Simone Hewitt shot 48% from the field. Soph guard Layla Noble, a Loyola transfer, should make an immediate impact.</p><h3>No. 4 Homewood-Flossmoor</h3><p>Four starters return from the 24-10 team that lost to Belleville East by seven in the Elite Eight: guards Toniya Brady, Laila Williams and Kate Jones along with 6-2 forward Ziko Okolo. Zoey Ratliff, a junior guard who missed last season with an ACL injury, is back.</p><h3>No. 5 Marist</h3><p>The RedHawks, who reached the 4A Sweet Sixteen last season, have been waiting for this year. They have 10 seniors, four in their fourth varsity season and three in their third. Lily Porter, Caroline Flynn and Grace Harmon are returning starters.</p><h3>No. 6 Loyola</h3><p>A pair of Division I recruits are back from last year's 4A runner-up. Senior forward Emily Naraky (12.8 ppg) is committed to Oakland, while senior guard/forward Maddie Locke (11.1 ppg) is committed to Brown. The Ramblers are young overall, but remain one of the state's elite programs.</p><h3>No. 7 Libertyville</h3><p>Villanova recruit Lily Fisher (19.8 ppg) leads four returning starters from a 27-7 Class 4A regional and conference champ. KateRyan Castro, Elle Knight and Addie Casey also return as regulars.</p><h3>No. 8 Benet</h3><p>Veteran assistant Kelsey Coulter takes over for longtime head coach Joe Kilbride and will build around returning starters Ava Mersinger, a senior point guard committed to Northern Illinois, and Lucy Tierney, a junior guard/forward. Like Nazareth, Marist and Carmel, Benet will join the powerhouse GCAC Red after the merger with the East Suburban Catholic.</p><h3>No. 9 Downers Grove North</h3><p>BYU recruit Campbell Thulin (15 ppg, 7 rpg) is back to lead a team that went 30-3 and lost to Nazareth in the sectional final last season. Junior guard Caitlin Sandridge and sophomore guard Eva Yerkovich are other key veterans.</p><h3>No. 10 St. Charles East</h3><p>Junior Brooklyn Schilb (21.7 ppg), who is the reigning DuKane Conference Player of the Year and has multiple Division I offers, is among four returning starters for a team that lost to Loyola in the Elite Eight. Junior point guard Kathlyn Bainbridge is another proven veteran.</p><h3>No. 11 Glenbard West</h3><p>Ellie Noble, a 6-0 senior committed to Northern Illinois, leads an experienced team coming off a 28-5 season that ended in the sectional final. Fellow seniors Sophia Evans, Lily Hubbuch, Katie Meehan, Lily Pones and Nina Hendricksen also return.</p><h3>No. 12 Carmel</h3><p>Liv Johnson, who averaged almost a double as a freshman last season, is one of the state's best players and is drawing plenty of high-major interest. The Corsairs went 25-10 and reached the 4A Elite Eight a year ago.</p><h3>No. 13 Lane</h3><p>There could be a changing of the guard in the Public League. Traditional powers Kenwood, Butler and Young all are inexperienced, but the Champions return all five starters from a city semifinalist and 4A regional champ. Junior Vega Ransom-Marks (13.5 ppg) is the top scorer back and junior Anais Harris (9.9 ppg, 7.6 rpg) is the top rebounder.</p><h3>No. 14 Trinity</h3><p>The Blazers are young, but want a Class 3A state title after finishing third last season. Keyera Gamble, a 6-2 junior, and senior point guard Destiny Sacluti are returning starters. Gamble, 6-0 junior wing Nayana Harper and 6-0 sophomore guard Destinie Roe are some of the state's top prospects in their classes.</p><h3>No. 15 Maine South</h3><p>The Hawks return six of their top nine players and 65% of their scoring from a 28-5 team that lost to Loyola in.the sectional final. Senior guards Hayden Fahy (12.8 ppg) and Gianna LaVecchia are returning starters.</p><h3>No. 16 Glenbrook South</h3><p>The Titans shared the Central Suburban South title last season with Evanston — whom they lost to in a regional final — and Maine South. Junior Niki Davorija has offers from DePaul and Murray State, while senior Norah Rodgers is committed to Division III Colorado College.</p><h3>No. 17 Peoria Richwoods</h3><p>The Knights could be the top team in Central Illinois and they should make some noise in Class 3A after losing to Belleville East in a 4A sectional final last season. They lost one DI prospect (Keniya Todd) via transfer, but have two more back in Londyn Sommerville (Creighton) and Kayla Herron.</p><h3>No. 18 Providence</h3><p>Four starters are back from a 31-5 team that lost to eventual 3A champ Washington in the Elite Eight. Layken Callahan, a 6-0 senior guard, is the top returning scorer. Also back as regulars are 6-0 senior Taylor Healy, 6-0 junior Kennady Kotowski and senior Olivia Anderson.</p><h3>No. 19 Prospect</h3><p>Division I recruit Zoe Black (Denver) is one of four starters back for the Knights, who won 21 games and a regional last season and have a new coach in Chris Keehn.</p><h3>No. 20 Rolling Meadows</h3><p>A strong senior group graduated from last year's Class 4A fourth-place finisher. The Mustangs will build around three senior guards —‚ Nellie Osterhues, last year's No. 2 scorer; Anna Andriano and Iris Jordan.</p><h3>No. 21 Fremd</h3><p>After graduating four starters, the Vikings will lean on a strong defense and their one returning regular: senior point guard and Miami (Ohio) commit Gracie Todd.</p><h3>No. 22 Bolingbrook</h3><p>The Raiders have the state's top freshman in Joy Pettigrew, whose offers already include Penn State, Miami, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio State, Louisville and Arizona State.</p><h3>No. 23 St. Viator</h3><p>The Lions won their first state trophy last season (fourth in 3A) and return their top four scorers: junior Ava Garcia, senior Bella Gounaris, senior Kalin McCrea and junior Evelyn Hill.</p><h3>No. 24 St. Ignatius</h3><p>Senior Kaylee Clark averaged 15 points and 10 rebounds for a team that lost to Nazareth in the sectional semifinals. Juniors Maeve Hickey, Ella Kueker and Paige Stumm also are proven veterans.</p><h3>25. Hersey</h3><p>Senior Sadie Marks leads the Huskies, who return six of their top seven players (including four starters) from a 21-8 regional champ.</p>

entries.title: Bears' defense has progressed this season, but is it championship-caliber?
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> were sure they had something special defensively in 2018.</p><p>With that side of the ball stacked, then further boosted by the trade for Khalil Mack going into the season, they were title-ready. All they needed was a decent offense.</p><p>That never came together, and the team wasted two seasons of elite defense as the other side of the ball wandered with coach Matt Nagy and quarterback Mitch Trubisky.</p><p>It was the opposite at Halas Hall this summer. The offense — including the trajectory of quarterback Caleb Williams — pointed upward under coach Ben Johnson, and the Bears hoped their defense could play well enough to get by.</p><p>The offense, indeed, has been one of the best in the league. And if the defense gets there, too, making a Super Bowl run would be very realistic.</p><p>The Bears had that in mind when they traded two first-round picks for star defensive tackle <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/05/new-bears-dt-jeffery-simmons-arrival-at-halas-hall-has-been-flawless-on-and-off-the-field" target="_blank" >Jeffery Simmons</a> last month. It was time to bring everything up to code and go for it.</p><p>As they head into their home game Sunday against the Saints, they aren’t there yet. The defense has gotten better since Week 1, when it allowed 37 points to the Panthers, but it still has work to do in key areas. It has been inconsistent against the run, and the best quarterbacks the Bears have faced have picked it apart (though that has improved since Simmons’ arrival).</p><p>The checklist for a championship-level defense starts with being tough to run against and tight in pass coverage, the latter of which also requiring a forceful pass rush. The Bears rank in the bottom half of the NFL in opponent passer rating (93.1) and yards per carry allowed (4.4).</p><p>Defensive tackle Grady Jarrett is fixated on that 4.4 number. It needs to be lower than four and ideally lower than 3.5.</p><p>One play can make all the difference in a game. The Bears would have held the Buccaneers to 3.7 yards per carry Nov. 8 had Bucky Irving’s 25-yard run in the fourth quarter not spiked it to 4.5. Nobody got to the gap on the left side, then Irving broke three tackles.</p><p>‘‘We’ve got to eliminate those things,’’ Jarrett said. ‘‘These one-off plays are throwing off our average.’’</p><p>Then there are the game-defining situations, such as third downs and trips to the red zone.</p><p>The Bears have been the best third-down defense in the league, holding opponents to a 22.8% conversion rate. The NFL record, according to Pro Football Reference, belongs to the 2019 Patriots at 24.1%.</p><p>In the red zone, the Bears have allowed touchdowns 53.8% of the time. That ranks 12th in the league.</p><p>It’s also essential to have a brilliant strategist running the defense, and Bears coordinator Dennis Allen has the résumé to claim that. Not only is he one of the most experienced defensive play-callers in the NFL, but he showed some savvy problem-solving skills in his first season and a half — before the Simmons trade — that the Bears lacked under Matt Eberflus, who ran the defense before him.</p><p>Those pieces are the foundation of a good defense, but it takes more to be great: blue-chip playmakers capable of taking over a game. The Bears have Simmons and nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon, but they need more than that.</p><p>They’re betting defensive end Montez Sweat rises to that level playing alongside Simmons, who draws double-teams and is constantly in his ear. And they hope safety Coby Bryant, who suffered a major knee injury in training camp, returns down the stretch or in the playoffs.</p><p>The Bears’ ultimate goal is to have a defense that can carry them in any given week if the offense sputters. It did against the Bucs, as Williams threw four interceptions and the ground game stalled, but that was against a bad team. The defense will be tested much more strenuously, with five of the Bears’ final seven games against teams in the top half of the league in total offense.</p><p>If the defense is as good as the Bears think, that’s a perfect ramp-up to the playoffs.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Bulls' Noa Essengue learning defense the hard way: One foul at a time
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — Noa Essengue can watch all the film he wants, read all the scouting reports his coaching staff uploads to his phone.</p><p>Once that heart rate jumps up to in-game 200 and that 7-foot-1 wiry wingspan starts to get looser than usual, the whistles start a blowing.</p><p>A major issue for the second-year forward as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls</a> are hellbent on turning a project into a defensive stopper. No easy task since Essengue entered Monday’s game with the Cavaliers leading the team in personal fouls with 38 — five more than Jalen Smith who has logged 130 more total minutes than his younger teammate.</p><p>The best way for Essengue to continue improving as a defender and cut that number down in his eyes? More reps and more experience. Film only does so much.</p><p>“Of course I need to watch film, not only before the game but after the game,” Essengue said. “It’s just as important to be ready after the game to see what you need to correct what went wrong, what went great. But what’s the most important is getting reps. The more reps you get, the more experience you get. Just get more reps.”</p><p>Coach Tiago Splitter agreed but also said there was more to it than that.</p><p>“Sometimes it’s a reputation that you need to have,” Splitter said. “Defensive players, they earn that with time. Yes, he’s got to be smarter, but it comes with time, experience, the referees knowing what you do and how you play. Taking care of your arms, he’s got long arms. Be smart with that.”</p><p>There is definitely something to Splitter’s assessment of player reputation. Being an elite defender is earned but also comes with a certain style of defending. Essengue's currently is he’s long and very young.</p><p>“It’s what they believe you are,” Splitter added of the officials giving certain players a longer leash. “Like let’s name a guy that I coached like Dillon Brooks – everybody knows that he’s physical. He’s going to be able to use his arms, his body in a different way than another guy. PJ Tucker, super physical. Those types of guys are going to be allowed to do a little bit more.”</p><p>So why is it so important for the Bulls to make Essengue into a wing stopper? Because they have one player that is elite at it in Isaac Okoro and he’s a free agent after the season.</p><p></p><h3><b>Humble beginnings</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>Splitter hasn’t always agreed with Kenny Atkinson’s coaching decisions, but he made it clear that he will always have respect for the Cleveland coach, especially since it was Atkinson that gave him his first coaching job back in Brooklyn in 2019.</p><p>“Kenny helped me to get a job basically in Brooklyn when he was the head coach,” Splitter said. “He was always super honest. I am the same way. We would fight or disagree on a lot of things. When you’re in those locker rooms or meetings with coaches you try to be honest and you sometimes have a different perspective.</p><p>“He taught me a lot about player development, how to prepare for games. Also, we were in a rebuild in Brooklyn, so how to keep the gym alive when you have a bad streak.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Spread thin</b></h3><h3></h3><p></p><p>According to historical point-spread records tracked by multiple betting sites, the 16.5-point spread that the Bulls had against them in Minnesota was one of the biggest upsets in the last few decades. News to Splitter but a stat he also found some humor in.</p><p>“Is that good or bad?” he said laughing. “We don’t pay attention to those things, but we knew we started the season the way we started, not very good, and those spreads start to get bigger and bigger.”</p>

entries.title: Lions must push ahead without defensive end Aidan Hutchinson
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — The Detroit Lions were close to having the perfect trip to Germany.</p><p>They beat the New England Patriots 35-10 and their offensive stars put on a display that Munich fans won't forget. Jahmyr Gibbs finished with 252 yards — 153 rushing and 99 receiving — and scored two touchdowns, while German citizen and fan favorite Amon-Ra St. Brown had 98 yards and two scores on four catches.</p><p>But there was one thing that went badly wrong. For the second time in three weeks, the Lions lost one of their defensive captains to a serious injury.</p><p>The team has no idea when linebacker Jack Campbell might play again after his severe neck injury two weeks ago, and now star defensive end Aidan Hutchinson has an injury to his right knee that will end his season, a person familiar with the situation told The Associated Press on Sunday night.</p><p>The Lions didn't have any media availability on Monday after their long flight back to Detroit and didn't make any announcement about Hutchinson's condition. The knee injury comes two years after he missed much of the 2024 season with a broken leg.</p><p>"When you lose a player like that, it hurts a little bit, but our guys stepped up and finished the game," coach Dan Campbell said. "This is the second time this has happened (this season), and our guys didn't bat an eye. We just went back to work, and that's not always an easy thing to do."</p><p>Hutchinson was hurt celebrating a sack of New England's Drake Maye, who suffered an ankle injury on the same play and did not return to the game. The Patriots were always going to have a hard time stopping Detroit's high-powered offense, but they looked helpless offensively after Maye left.</p><p>The Lions likely won't have as easy of a time in their four remaining division games. Now they'll have to navigate the tough NFC North without Campbell and Hutchinson.</p><h3>Easier road gets rougher </h3><h3></h3><p>After a terrible start to the season, the Lions' defense has played well over the last three games, holding Minnesota, Miami and New England to an average of 11.3 points.</p><p>Those weren't the most dangerous offenses in the league, and now Detroit gets the Tampa Bay Buccaneers with a banged-up Baker Mayfield.</p><p>After that, though, the Lions face the Bears on Thanksgiving Day — the first of two meetings this season with Caleb Williams. Detroit also has matchups with the Vikings and the Packers, and will need players to step up and replace Campbell against the run and Hutchinson on the pass rush.</p><h3>Next man up </h3><h3></h3><p>Rookie defensive end Derrick Moore looks like he will be the first option to replace Hutchinson. Detroit's second-round pick has four sacks after starting the season only getting a few snaps as a rotation player.</p><p>He played 67.8% of Detroit's defensive snaps on Sunday, recording his second straight two-sack game.</p>

entries.title: No point of contention for Bulls, who fall in Cleveland
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND — The Bulls still aren’t interested in moral victories. How about at least staying competitive?</p><p>They’re more than open to that, especially after spending the first three weeks of the season as ‘‘the other team’s lunch,’’ as guard Buddy Hield put it.</p><p>Although their two-game winning streak came to an end Monday with a 126-115 loss to the Cavaliers, victory was within reach — straining on tiptoes, but still within reach — until midway through the fourth quarter.</p><p>Point guard Josh Giddey felt he was the reason the Bulls couldn’t make it happen. He was on the bench throughout the second half and didn’t need much explanation from coach Tiago Splitter as to why on a night when he went 1-for-5 shooting with six turnovers.</p><p>‘‘[I] didn’t have it, clearly, from the start,’’ Giddey said after the game. ‘‘Just didn’t come to play, wasn’t ready, and that’s what happens against a good team like that.</p><p>‘‘There’s plays I think I can make. Some nights they come in a positive way, and some nights, like [Monday], they don’t. Sloppy with the ball against an active team, and it was on me. It was just bad from the start, all around. Turnovers, defense, everything. I just want to put it in the trash and move on.’’</p><p>Splitter agreed about moving on but said he doesn’t intend to change the starting lineup, even after backup point guard Tre Jones again played at a high level, finishing with 16 points and zero turnovers.</p><p>‘‘[Giddey] didn’t have a good night,’’ Splitter said. ‘‘Sometimes it happens. You don’t have it, and you go from there. He was doing a great job passing the ball, [but overall] he just didn’t have it. But it’s not just Josh. It’s a collective thing. We win together, we lose together.’’</p><p>Fortunately, Splitter also sees the Bulls (3-10) playing better defense together since their awful eight-game losing streak.</p><p>‘‘There’s a lot of things we’ve been preaching, and sometimes it takes some time,’’ he said. ‘‘The team just has good momentum right now, a good vibe. We want to get stops. We know how hard it is to get stops in the NBA.’’</p><p>Some nights are harder than others. The Bulls’ upset victory Saturday in Minneapolis was made somewhat easier by the Timberwolves shooting 9-for-38 (24%) from three-point range. The night before, the Hawks shot 8-for-40 (20%) from three-point range as the Bulls triumphed at the United Center.</p><p>The Cavaliers weren’t as helpful. Seven-time All-Star guard Donovan Mitchell finished with a game-high 39 points — including a ridiculous 20 points on 8-for-8 shooting in the fourth quarter — and the Cavs finished 10-for-33 (30.3%) from long range while also dominating in the paint, scoring 68 points on 51-for-97 shooting (53%) from the field.</p><p>Still, even when it seemed the Bulls were losing their grip late, they squeezed out one more attempt. Forward Matas Buzelis made a three-pointer with 3:03 left to pull the Bulls within 11. After Splitter successfully challenged a turnover, guard Norman Powell made a floater to cut the deficit to nine. Buzelis and Powell scored to trim the deficit to six before the Cavs apparently decided enough was enough. Center Jarrett Allen threw down a dunk with 1:27 left. After Buzelis missed a three, Mitchell made a running layup to extend the Cavs’ lead back to 10.</p><p>Although improvements are being made, the young Bulls aren’t there yet.</p><p>‘‘We are more connected [defensively],’’ Splitter said. ‘‘The whole wheel has to be connected on defense, and, in that regard, we have been better the last four games, let’s say.’’</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Departing friend wants to deliver parting shot
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I've been friends with a married couple for over 40 years and knew them both before they knew each other. She's popular, has a great sense of humor and is an excellent wife, mother, grandmother, neighbor, etc. I actually became "friends" with the husband first (quotes because he basically forced his friendship on me).</p><p>Recently, I realized I like her more than I like him, and I know she likes me. (She mentioned it to him before they married.) He has some character issues and has cheated on her in the past. It's my belief that if I were to continue being friends with them, there would be an affair. (These things tend to sneak up on people.)</p><p>I'm semi-retired and ready to move to a warmer climate, and I want to have closure in our friendship to avoid a future awkward moment. I think the best way is to explain to them at the same time that the reason for my avoidance is because I am fonder of her than him. How do you recommend I address this issue? — <i>CHARACTER WINS ESTEEM</i></p><p><b>DEAR CHARACTER:</b> This type of "closure" would serve no constructive purpose. His infidelity is none of your business, and it's not your place to teach him a lesson about character. Instead of hurting your friend's feelings at the moment you exit his life, bid him and his wife a fond farewell, thanking them both for all the good memories you share. Do not maintain contact with the wife after you move. An affair can't "sneak up" on you unless you leave the door open.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm a first-time grandma. I'd like to move back to Texas to be closer to my grandbabies. My family all lives here in California, including my mom. My adult kids have amazing jobs where they are. It would just be easier for my husband and me to move back so I can be with them.</p><p>My brother and all his children and grandchildren live close to where Mom is living, so she won't be left alone. I would like for her to come meet her great-grandkids as she has done with my brother's grandkids, but she doesn't want to do it because she feels her great-grandchildren here wouldn't know her. I am asking only for her to come live with me a few months to get to see the little ones. Am I a bad person for wanting to have my time now with all my kids? — <i>PLANNING A MOVE</i></p><p><b>DEAR PLANNING:</b> You are not a "bad person" for wanting to establish a relationship with your grandchildren. There is a defined role that grandparents can play in a child's life. However, due to the complications of age, great-grandparents can be forgiven for not wanting to play a similar role. If your mother is up there in age and reluctant to travel, don't force it. Go, enjoy your time with your grandchildren, visit your mother as often as is feasible and bring pictures and videos for her to enjoy.</p><p>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127. </p>

entries.title: Chicago renters struggle to keep up with gas and water bills as landlords switch to new way of billing
entries.summary: <p>When Maiko Lehman moved into her two-bedroom, seventh-floor apartment in Chicago’s Edgewater neighborhood in 2022, she was thrilled with the updated kitchen and all the windows in the corner unit.</p><p>She had to get a roommate so she could afford her bills, but the two of them knew exactly what they owed the landlord every month: the rent plus a flat fee of $100 to cover gas, water and trash services.</p><p>“It was a known fee,” said Lehman, 56. “It was in the lease, and you knew it when you moved in.”</p><p>Then, in 2024, the building changed hands, and property management announced it would start using a “ratio utility billing system” — better known as RUBS.</p><p>The landlord outsourced the billing to a third-party company called Conservice, which splits up the master gas, sewer and water bills according to a formula based on the size of the apartment, the number of occupants, and other factors. Conservice then tacks on a service fee and sends the bill out to renters.</p><p>Since her building switched to RUBS, Lehman’s monthly utility bills have ranged from $88.05 to $225.57. She never knows what the total bill will be — nor is she sure the property management isn’t charging more than it should. She’s tried to get them to tell her the formula, but to no avail.</p><p>She said she can try to conserve gas and water, but she’s still charged based on whatever the totals are for the entire property. If there are leaky toilets or drafty windows throughout the building, it’s her and her neighbors — not the landlord — bearing the cost for the higher utility bills. In fact, Lehman thinks RUBS disincentivizes management from making timely repairs.</p><p>Many of her neighbors with limited incomes are struggling, and some have even had to move out, Lehman added.</p><p>“There's people in the building now who are flirting with [whether] they can afford the rent, and all of a sudden, this month the bill is higher for the utilities,” she said.</p><p>WBEZ reached out to Berkshire Residential, the property manager for Lehman’s building, but has not received a response.</p><p>Lehman is among the estimated tens of thousands of Chicago renters living in a building that uses RUBS. Consumer advocates and tenant organizations say this way of billing is becoming more of a trend in master-metered apartment buildings all over the city — those buildings that don’t have separate water and gas meters for each unit. And as utility costs continue to climb, tenants are trying to keep up with the fluctuating bills while struggling to get answers from their landlords. Furthermore, experts say there is little recourse for tenants because existing laws on utility billing don’t go far enough.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Maiko Lehman says ratio utility billing — better known as RUBS — has made her monthly bills unpredictable. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Esther Yoon-Ji Kang/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>A lack of regulation</h3><p>Neither Chicago’s Department of Buildings nor the Department of Housing tracks how many buildings use ratio utility billing.</p><p>In the majority of these master-metered apartment buildings, landlords still estimate the costs and bake them into the rent — or they charge a consistent, flat fee on top of rent that is disclosed in the lease.</p><p>But experts say rising utility costs, plus the proliferation of companies like Conservice that offer property management software and billing services, which are heavily marketed to owners, are pushing more landlords to switch to RUBS.</p><p>“RUBS basically shifts risk of volatile, rising utility costs off of the landlords and onto the tenants,” said Olivia Wein, a senior attorney at the National Consumer Law Center. “There are now many RUBS companies developing these products for landlords. At the same time, people are experiencing unaffordability — the cost of everything is going up.”</p><p>Now, more and more apartment renters are getting bills from companies like Conservice, Yes Energy Management, and Synergy Utility BIlling.</p><p>Wein said there are currently no laws in Illinois that ban the use of RUBS, and there is no agency regulating the billing companies.</p><p>A spokesperson for the Illinois Commerce Commission, which regulates utility companies, said in a statement that it “does not have authority over ratio metering. This would be a tenant-landlord matter.”</p><p>Wein, with NCLC, said “because of the lack of transparency and the newness of [RUBS], and the lack of a clear regulator in this space, it's an opportunity for abuses to proliferate.”</p><p>Illinois has some laws on the books related to utility billing, but Wein said they don’t go far enough. For example, Illinois requires landlords give notice to tenants before switching to RUBS, and renters have a right to see the master utility bills. The city of Chicago does not have RUBS-related ordinances on the books, although Mayor Brandon Johnson’s <a class="Link" href="https://occprodstoragev1.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/matterattachmentspublic/fc55c4ab-2a19-4a39-8ae9-2dfc65e0c381.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Protecting Renters Ordinance</u></a>, currently before City Council, seeks to codify some of the same protections as the state laws.</p><p>Meanwhile, organizations like NCLC, as well as tenant rights and legal aid groups, have said they are getting more calls from frustrated tenants who can’t get answers from their landlords about their RUBS bills. And for now, there is little recourse because it’s difficult to find lawyers to take on cases related to RUBS, and it’s not easy to organize a tenant union to take collective action.</p><p>Conservice did not respond to questions about its billing services. The company’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.bbb.org/us/ut/river-heights/profile/billing-services/conservice-utility-management-billing-1126-22011873/customer-reviews" target="_blank" ><u>page</u></a> on the Better Business Bureau website has received more than 150 reviews that average one out of five stars.</p><p>WBEZ also reached out to landlord groups in Chicago. The Neighborhood Building Owners Alliance said only about 10% of its members use RUBS in their buildings.</p><p>A spokesperson for the Illinois Apartment Association, another landlord and property manager organization, said in a statement: “RUBS provides an accurate estimate based on actual usage. A fair, transparent, and consistent RUBS formula promotes resident conservation, encourages responsible utility usage, and creates management efficiencies that reduce upward pressure on rent.”</p><p>But consumer advocates and tenant groups say that’s not true.</p><p>“The tenant's bill is not tied to actual tenant usage,” Wein said.</p><p>In some cases, tenants would go out of town for weeks but return to higher gas and water bills.</p><p>Wein said the issue extends beyond Illinois. Several states and municipalities throughout the U.S. have tried to address challenges related to RUBS with varying degrees of success. She said some states, like Connecticut, have <a class="Link" href="https://www.ctinsider.com/news/article/ct-supreme-court-apartments-utility-bills-meters-19462606.php" target="_blank" ><u>banned</u></a> RUBS; others limit landlords to using specific formulas and have an agency that settles landlord-tenant disputes. Currently, there are also efforts in cities like <a class="Link" href="https://www.seattletimes.com/business/real-estate/seattle-renters-landlords-clash-over-ratio-utility-billing-system/" target="_blank" ><u>Seattle</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-08-26/la-renters-are-billed-for-shared-utilities-some-wont-pay-until-they-can-see-math" target="_blank" ><u>Los Angeles</u></a> to ban the use of ratio utility billing systems.</p><p>“It is very hard to craft a comprehensive consumer protection law when it comes to [RUBS],” Wein said, adding that this billing practice could lead to more evictions throughout the country. “Really the safest thing to do to protect tenant housing affordability is just to prohibit the practice right now.”</p><h3>Tenants fight back</h3><p>Ending this billing practice is exactly what 85-year-old Viola Davis wants.</p><p>She first moved into the Oglesby Towers high-rise in Chicago’s South Shore neighborhood eight years ago. For years, she paid a flat fee of $105 for utilities on top of her rent for her one-bedroom apartment.</p><p>“I thought when I moved here, I could afford this building,” Davis said.</p><p>Since early this year, when her landlord, Stuart Handler and TLC Management, switched the building to RUBS, Davis has had to pay anything from around $150 to more than $220 in utilities per month.</p><p>She has struggled to make ends meet using her pension and social security funds, not knowing whether she’ll have enough to buy her groceries or give her great grandson his birthday money.</p><p>So Davis started talking to her neighbors — many of them fellow senior citizens on a fixed income — and found that some saw bills as high as $500.</p><p>The neighbors contacted community organizing nonprofit Southside Together and formed a tenant union. They held their first press conference in August, and sent a letter to TLC demanding a meeting.</p><p>Housing organizer Savannah Brown said the tenants’ efforts led to management reversing a trash fee, but that the group will continue to push to get rid of RUBS.</p><p>“RUBS is essentially a variable rent increase,” Brown said. “This is just another thing to push out folks who have been in the neighborhood for the longest, who have been in this building for decades.”</p><p>WBEZ reached out to Handler and TLC Management but has not received a response.</p><p>Last month, the Oglesby tenants held a second press conference. One resident, 63-year-old Antoinette Gray, said she was being evicted because she couldn’t keep up with the bills.</p><p>"When Stuart Handler started RUBS, it had a real impact on me, my life, everything,” Gray said. “I’ve done the best I could to stay here. Their response has been, ‘If you can't pay, just leave.’”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Where to dine in and order carryout for Thanksgiving 2026
entries.summary: <p>Depending on your relationship with your kitchen, Thanksgiving is either your idea of cooking nirvana or a chore to be avoided at all costs. No matter where you land, this list of restaurants has your needs covered, from dine-in spots where even the cleanup is left in someone else’s hands to carryout packages where your secret is safe with us. Just need a sweet ending? There are plenty of places for pies and desserts too. Be sure to get your orders in early as most spots require reservations.</p><h2>Where to dine in</h2><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://ascionebistro.com/" target="_blank" ><b>Ascione</b></a></h3><p>1500 E. 55th St., and 8006 Lincoln Ave., Skokie<br><a class="Link" href="https://ascionebistro.com/" target="_blank" >ascionebistro.com</a></p><p>Thanksgiving is all about comfort, and this modern Italian restaurant — with locations in Hyde Park and Skokie — understands that perfectly. From its white table-clothed tables and welcoming service to its hearty portions, it’s unfussy in all the right ways. <b>I</b>ts prices are easy on the wallet, including Thanksgiving, which is something to be grateful for.<br><b>What’s on the menu:</b> While Ascione’s three-course Thanksgiving lunch menu ($49) may lack in options, it features upgraded versions of all the traditional holiday dishes. For starters, choose from butternut squash soup or Mediterranean salad. The brioche stuffing with parsnips and sage complements the roast turkey. Of course, there’s cranberry sauce as well as green beans and mashed and sweet potatoes. You could opt for pumpkin pie, but the <i>cioccolato</i> (chocolate) cake with strawberries is hard to pass up.<br><b>How to reserve</b>: Kick off the holiday early here with reservations on <a class="Link" href="https://ascionebistro.com/contact-us/" target="_blank" ><u>resy.com</u></a> starting at 11:30 a.m. and ending at 2:45 p.m.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.eataly.com/us_en/stores/chicago" target="_blank" ><b><u>Eataly Chicago</u></b></a></h3><p><b>43 E. Ohio St.</b><br><a class="Link" href="https://www.eataly.com/restaurants/chicago" target="_blank" >eataly.com/restaurants/chicago</a></p><p>Italy may not be the first place you think of when Thanksgiving rolls around, but this multistoried love letter to all things from “The Boot” is working hard to change that line of thinking with both a dine-in option and to-go meals. And procrastinators take note: Eataly will be open 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. on Thanksgiving for all your Italian shopping needs.<br><b>What’s on the menu:</b> The three-course meal ($58) offered at La Pizza & La Pasta starts with a fall salad before moving on to options like butternut squash ravioli or lobster linguine (+$25) for the first course. Choose from roasted turkey breast, red wine-braised beef or oven-roasted branzino (+$25) for the main course served with traditional sides. Save room for the apple and almond tarts served with almond streusel and flor di latte gelato (+$12).<br><b>How to reserve:</b> Grab a table on <a class="Link" href="https://www.opentable.com/r/la-pizza-and-la-pasta-eataly-chicago" target="_blank" ><u>OpenTable</u></a> or order to-go packages <a class="Link" href="https://catering.eataly.com/items/folder/thanksgiving-2026" target="_blank" ><u>here</u></a>.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://thehawksmoor.com/us/locations/chicago/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Hawksmoor</u></b></a></h3><p><b>500 N. La Salle Dr.</b><br><a class="Link" href="https://thehawksmoor.com/us/locations/chicago/" target="_blank" >thehawksmoor.com/us/locations/chicago/</a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> like Yorkshire pudding and cauliflower cheese. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Set inside a historic, multilevel building with restored barrel-vaulted ceilings and jewel-toned velvet booths, this British import is offering a Thanksgiving version of its Sunday-only prime rib roast supper ($150) for the holiday. Its a la carte menu, with signature dishes like steak tartare and steaks galore, is on offer too as well as standard Sunday Roast ($75).<br><b>What’s on the menu:</b> Cooked over an open fire, that dry-aged hunk of meat served family-style is paired with Brit-leaning sides like Yorkshire pudding and cauliflower cheese. Potatoes are showered with beef jus. Pair with a proper bone marrow gravy and horseradish, the latter adding some zing to the meal. Might we suggest sticky toffee pudding with ice cream to finish?<br><b>How to reserve</b>: Book a table between 11:45 a.m. to 8 p.m. on <a class="Link" href="https://thehawksmoor.com/us/reservations/" target="_blank" ><u>OpenTable</u></a>.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.theiveschicago.com/" target="_blank" ><b><u>The Ives</u></b></a></h3><p><b>12 S. Chinese green vegetables in a bechamel sauce are topped with breadcrumbs, her version of green bean casserole, while wild rice gets an upgrade courtesy of maitake and shiitake mushrooms. Vegetarian packages are available as well ($136).<br><b>How to reserve:</b> Order on <a class="Link" href="https://www.toasttab.com/catering/noodle-bird-2957-west-diversey-avenue/menu/thanksgiving%20packages%3A%202026/" target="_blank" ><u>Toast</u></a> for pickup Nov. 25-26.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.santamasa.com/" target="_blank" >Santa Masa Tamaleria</a></h3><p>7544 W. Addison St.<br><a class="Link" href="https://www.santamasa.com/" target="_blank" >santamasa.com</a></p><p>As its name indicates, this casual Dunning spot embraces housemade masa in numerous ways, including for its tamales — and its Thanksgiving to-go menu is no different.<br><b>What’s on the menu:</b> Mix and match from six varieties of tamales available by the dozen or in trays of 30. Trays of beef barbacoa, chicken tinga, pozole verde and enchiladas suizas are on offer too. Sides range from chorizo verde stuffing to sweet potatoes with a salsa macha glaze. Quench your thirst with atole, café de olla or agua de jamaica, available in half and full gallon portions.<br><b>How to reserve:</b> Call 312-982-9306 or email (santamasachicago@gmail.com) for pickup on Nov. 25.</p><hr><p></p><h2>The sweet spots: Where to pick up dessert</h2><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.cafeyaya.com/" target="_blank" >Cafe Yaya</a></h3><p>2431 N. For Thanksgiving, owner Sandra Holl puts her flaky crusts to work in sweet pies like apple crumble and honey caramel pumpkin as well as savory offerings, including turkey pot pie and green bean casserole galette. Preorder online for pickup Nov. 23-25.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/guillotinebakery/?hl=en" target="_blank" >Guillotine Bakery</a></h3><p>1711 W. For its first Thanksgiving, it’s going big — literally! — with large-format offerings like kouign amann, vanilla and praline flan, and sourdough loaf. Preorder online for pickup Nov. 25 and 26.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.loafloungechicago.com/" target="_blank" >Loaf Lounge</a></h3><p>2934 N. On the sweet side, look for fruit-filled Danish, cinnamon rolls and seasonal cookies. Impress family members with “The Bear” famous chocolate cake. entries.title: Kyle Kinane returns with Kinanesgiving at Thalia Hall
entries.summary: <p>When stand-up comedians receive top billing on a show, they often remain backstage until the other acts have sufficiently warmed up the audience and they can be introduced to much fanfare.</p><p>Things operate differently at Kinanesgiving, an annual series at Thalia Hall in the lead-up to Thanksgiving. Comedian Kyle Kinane — born, raised, and trained in the Chicago area — is the headliner and booker, but pops out at the beginning to thank everyone for coming and talk up the line-up.</p><p>Kinane wants none of the other comics to assume the unpleasant task of going up cold. Later, he’ll close out the evening after spending the run-up watching the others from the wings, visibly tickled by each performance.</p><p>“I book the show as one I’d want to watch; and then, I say it every year, but I realize I’ve screwed myself because I have to go up last,” says Kinane, 49, who has performed stand-up since 1999 and now resides in Portland, Oregon. “That’s the best review I can give to a show: I have so much fun watching it that I forget I have to go on.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-portrait-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a10000" name="module-a10000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Kinanesgiving</b><br><br><b>Where:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.thaliahallchicago.com/" target="_blank" >Thalia Hall,</a> 1808 S. Allport St.<br><b>When:</b> Nov. 23-24, 8 p.m.<br><b>Info:</b> Sold out; limited number of tickets available at the door for $45</div> </div><p>Kinanesgiving started in 2017 and has returned to Thalia Hall each year except for 2020 amid the height of COVID-19 precautions. This year’s series runs Monday, Nov. 23 and Tuesday, Nov. 24 marking the 16th and 17th Kinanesgivings, respectively. Each will feature Kinane and three-to-four other comics — and the event has built a reputation as featuring some up-and-comers audiences may want to pay attention to next.</p><p>Kinane, whose Rip Van Winkle beard and grizzled combat veteran voice belie a teddy bear underneath, certainly delights himself at Kinanesgiving. But he’s also offering less-seasoned comics the chance to perform at a sizable venue for a receptive crowd. The opportunity fits longstanding Chicago comedy tradition of elevating the work of peers and progeny.</p><p>Kinanesgiving shows are cheerful homecoming affairs. The audience hardly needs to be warmed up at all; it’s full of comedy fans who are generous with laughter and eager to add new comics to their Rolodex. (Kinane’s voice lives rent-free in their brains, too, since he provided voiceover for the ubiquitous Comedy Central promos of the 2010s.) This year’s performers include Chicago comics Sohrab Forouzesh, Tory Ward, and DJ Rybski; plus, Sean Patton and Shane Torres are using their Milwaukee tour dates as excuses to swing by.</p><p>The concept for Kinanesgiving came about because Kinane was looking to kill two birds with one plane ticket. While living in Los Angeles in November 2015, he performed a weekend at Second City’s UP Comedy Club and liked how he could extend the trip into Thanksgiving and visit family in Addison. Two years later, he tried to make those circumstances align, but UP wasn’t available. His booking agent suggested Thalia Hall, a 600-person venue in Chicago’s Pilsen neighborhood.</p><p>The theater was an instant hit, particularly due to the ways its staff make Kinane feel welcome. The green room is decorated in fall décor, including a handmade crochet banner courtesy of a Thalia Hall staffer. The comedian also appreciates goodies from First Slice Pie Café and how staff stock his favorite tequila, lay out a large charcuterie board and hand out fuzzy Thalia Hall socks to all the performers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-520000" name="image-520000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e20ba3e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6240x3502+0+329/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F05%2F22e9824c44a6912ace2bb8ba99b8%2F20181120-img-0187.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8080b78/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6240x3502+0+329/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F05%2F22e9824c44a6912ace2bb8ba99b8%2F20181120-img-0187.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9c3a11d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6240x3502+0+329/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F05%2F22e9824c44a6912ace2bb8ba99b8%2F20181120-img-0187.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Kyle Kinane performs in front of a crowd at Thalia Hall. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9c3a11d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6240x3502+0+329/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F05%2F22e9824c44a6912ace2bb8ba99b8%2F20181120-img-0187.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c991c7c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6240x3502+0+329/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F05%2F22e9824c44a6912ace2bb8ba99b8%2F20181120-img-0187.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9c3a11d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6240x3502+0+329/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F8f%2F05%2F22e9824c44a6912ace2bb8ba99b8%2F20181120-img-0187.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“I book the show as one I’d want to watch,” said Kinane, who began his stand-up career in the late 1990s. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Photo by Kris Lori </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kinane’s affinity for Thalia Hall goes both ways. “Kinanesgiving is the unofficial kickoff of the holiday season for all of us at this point,” says Bobby Ramirez, talent buyer for Thalia Hall. “Kinanesgiving shows always feel like you're hanging out with an old friend in your living room, having one of those nights that you don't want to end.”</p><p>Though Kinane lives on the West Coast now, he still keeps an eye on rising Chicago talent through friends, comics he’s caught thumbing through Instagram, or fellow stand-ups asking directly. When he comes to town outside of Kinanesgiving, he’ll sometimes pop into The Lincoln Lodge, an independent stand-up theater on Milwaukee Avenue, and watch the other comics on the bill.</p><p>“Whether [comics at Kinanesgiving] know each other or not, I want everybody to be friends,” Kinane says. “Like, ‘I know we’re all awkward weirdos, but the green room is a safe place for all of us.’ Everybody should make bonds and be like, ‘Next time I’m in your town, I’ll put you on my show, and vice versa.’”</p><p>Because the line-up is booked by a fellow comedian, others on the bill have permission to get silly — whether it’s trying some new material or veering off-script to playfully mess with an earlier performer. “A lineup curated by comedians is very fun because you get to watch people play off each other,” says Forouzesh, making his Kinanesgiving debut this year. “Kyle’s audience is people who revere comedy, meaning it’s a fun place to stretch your legs.”</p><p>“Gigs like this,” Forouzesh adds, “are good for the soul.” Same for audiences laughing with Kinane and his comic pals new and old.<br></p>

entries.title: Chaz Ebert still runs rogerebert.com. But she has plans for a musical
entries.summary: <p>Chaz Ebert is still in love with the movies.</p><p>One of the first to arrive at the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2026/10/15/chicago-international-film-festival-celebrity-movie-red-carpet-john-c-reilly-derrick-rose" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago International Film Festival</u></a> this year, she remained a constant presence, winding through crowds at AMC Newcity. She took in several screenings, from the French drama “All of a Sudden” to the John Malkovich-led comedy “Wild Horse Nine.”</p><p>She was visibly shaken upon leaving Alex Gibney’s “Musk,” a nearly four-hour documentary on the widespread influence of controversial tech billionaire Elon Musk. Calling the film a “gut punch,” she was resolved to find some way to help circumvent his global, “concentrated power.”</p><p>“Those are the things that Roger and I used to talk about,” she said of her late husband, the famed Chicago Sun-Times film critic Roger Ebert.</p><p>“What is it that we can do, or who can we help if we feel that we don't have the power and the authority to do it? Let's find out who does and let's help them.”</p><p>Those are constant questions for Chaz, who oversees several enterprises in honor of her spouse, including the Roger and Chaz Ebert Foundation and the criticism website <a class="Link" href="http://rogerebert.com" target="_blank" ><u>rogerebert.com</u></a>. She spends her days approving projects, such as the <a class="Link" href="https://siskelandebertstatue.org/" target="_blank" ><u>fundraising campaign</u></a> for a life-sized, bronze sculpture of the icon and his partner-in-criticism, Gene Siskel. There is also a documentary, play and biopic in the works about the friends — and sometimes foes — who taped their first TV review show <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/movies-and-tv/2025/11/04/film-events-mark-50th-anniversary-of-siskel-and-eberts-pairing-on-tv" target="_blank" ><u>more than 50 years ago</u></a>.</p><div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Roger and Chaz Ebert pictured at the Chicago Cultural Center in 2005. “She fills my horizon, she is the great fact of my life,” Roger wrote in his memoir, “Life Itself.” </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jim Frost/Sun-Times.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But Chaz also is leaning into her own creative and charitable pursuits. In recent years, she has directed a short documentary “The Wellness Warrior,” about health guru Deborah Szekely, and penned the book “It’s Time to Give a FECK,” about four key values: forgiveness, empathy, compassion and kindness. In 2027, she will host the second-annual FECK Awards in Chicago to honor inspirational leaders. And she helps fund the Chicago International Film Festival’s Black Perspectives program celebrating films by African Americans and those throughout the African diaspora.</p><p>She’s also busy writing a musical, a “Jesus Christ Superstar”-inspired tale about the Virgin Mary.</p><p>“It seems like life is pushing me,” said Chaz, who lives on the Near North Side. “I realize that this is the time for me to stop working on so many other people’s projects and just concentrate on what’s really important for me.”</p><h2>Finding love, security and laughter</h2><p>Chaz and Roger Ebert met in 1989. Chaz had already built a successful career as an attorney, and had two children from a previous marriage. Roger, who had never married, had already won a Pulitzer Prize for criticism and established himself as a TV star as part of the “Siskel & Ebert” program.</p><p>“He was so charming and so smart and so funny and a no-B.S. kind of guy, and I was attracted to that,” Chaz said in a <a class="Link" href="https://open.spotify.com/episode/3ewibrxYDvGzcDLlcl0xjZ" target="_blank" ><u>podcast interview</u></a>.</p><p>The couple wed in 1992<b>. </b>Roger called her “the love of my life” in his 2011 memoir, “Life Itself.”</p><p>“Her presence fills me with love and a deep security,” <a class="Link" href="https://www.rogerebert.com/roger-ebert/roger-loves-chaz" target="_blank" ><u>he wrote</u></a>. “That’s what a marriage is for.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Roger Ebert, pictured with Chaz, receives a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2005. The couple built an empire that now comprises the Ebert Company, Ebert Digital, Ebert Productions and the Roger and Chaz Ebert Foundation.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Frazer Harrison/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Together, they built an empire that withstood his death, and is now represented by a suite of businesses including the Ebert Company, Ebert Digital and Ebert Productions. They also traveled the world, met Hollywood icons and collected funny memories, which Chaz shares generously. For example, there’s the very first time that she met Siskel, who’d learned that her favorite movie was Stanley Kubrick’s “A Clockwork Orange.”</p><p>“Gene says, ‘Hello, Chaz. Did you know that Roger didn't like ‘A Clockwork Orange?’” Chaz recalled, laughing. “I said, ‘Oh, and this is how you greet me?’”</p><p>Chaz also told the story of visiting Kubrick’s gravesite on his estate in England with Roger. One of Kubrick’s pet donkeys bit Roger’s hand, but he declined to go to the hospital.</p><p>“The skin is not broken,” he said. “I think it makes a better story to say Stanley Kubrick's donkey bit me."</p><p>Roger loved to recount the event.</p><p>“He used to dine out on that all the time,” Chaz said.</p><p>The couple remained married until Roger’s death in 2013, following a long battle with cancer. Chaz helped him navigate multiple surgeries and complications, which left him unable to eat, drink or speak.</p><p>“She hung in there through a lot of tough times,” said longtime friend Carolyn Chambless, of West Town. “It was something that broke your heart, but also showed the strength and beauty in their relationship.”</p><h2>Leading rogerebert.com through change</h2><p>In Roger’s absence, Chaz was left trying to maintain rogerebert.com as a leading voice in film criticism.</p><p>Getting that respect initially had been an uphill battle. When the site launched in 2002, critics for print publications were more highly regarded.</p><p>“Back then, Roger had to fight to get the studios to allow the online film critics to be admitted to the movie screenings and to have their work quoted,” Chaz said.</p><p>But after his death, she had to navigate new challenges, including the ups and downs of the digital media landscape and expanding a stable of diverse critics who write with the authority of the site’s namesake<b>. </b>Google’s change to algorithms, which deprioritized traffic to news sites, has been among the recent ones. She said she has stayed afloat by remaining frugal and relying on ad revenue.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chaz Ebert remains a force in film in her own right and a constant presence at the city’s biggest movie events, including the Chicago International Film Festival, now in its 62nd year.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>She has received generous offers to sell the website, but can’t bear to see someone else control content tied so closely to her late husband’s name.</p><p>“If it were named something other than rogerebert.com, I would have sold it,” she said. “I have some really good editors across the country. It's easier to keep it going now.”</p><p>Though the film criticism landscape is changing, audiences appreciate the brand’s commitment to smart, high-quality reviews, Chaz said. In fact, the website is seeing an increase in traffic. That includes a large segment of younger readers, amid a <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/10/movies/movie-theaters-gen-z.html" target="_blank" ><u>resurgence</u></a> of interest in film among those under 30.</p><p>“Whenever I travel anywhere in the world to other film festivals, somebody always comes up to me and says, ‘We love rogerebert.com,’ and so that makes me feel good,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-dc0000" name="image-dc0000"></a> a recent bout with long pneumonia also prompted her to get serious about taking time to realize her own dream projects. She is especially passionate about writing her Mary musical, which explores<b> </b>“the return of divine feminine compassion to the world.”</p><p>In addition to hosting the FECK Awards, Chaz also has given back by donating to charities, highlighting Black and women writers at rogerebert.com, and previously sponsoring an award for new directors at the Chicago International Film Festival.</p><p>She said she tries to lead with empathy, which Roger believed was an intrinsic part of the movie-going experience.</p><p>Watching a film allows you to walk in the shoes of people from different backgrounds, she said.</p><p>“Chaz understands the power of Roger’s legacy,” said Mimi Plauché, artistic director of the Chicago International Film Festival. “[She] is so dedicated to continuing that work. Wells Drive at Harold Washington Library." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7cb6573/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3698x2075+0+195/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F93%2Faa%2F2d80ba4148f788977d65e965cd1e%2Fmitchell-021219-07.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/06195ed/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3698x2075+0+195/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F93%2Faa%2F2d80ba4148f788977d65e965cd1e%2Fmitchell-021219-07.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7cb6573/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3698x2075+0+195/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F93%2Faa%2F2d80ba4148f788977d65e965cd1e%2Fmitchell-021219-07.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chaz Ebert gives the keynote speech at a ceremony and sign unveiling for Ida B. Wells Drive at Harold Washington Library in February 2019. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Rich Hein/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Chaz’s desire to help others was formed during her childhood on the Near West Side<b>.</b> From 6 years old, she would tag along as her mother, a precinct captain, encouraged their neighbors to vote.</p><p>She later graduated from DePaul University’s College of Law and worked for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission before leading the Ebert enterprises.</p><p>She said she would like to get more involved in the social justice sector, amid the Trump administration’s Civil Rights rollbacks and dismantling of federal agencies through the Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency.</p><p>“It makes me want to scream,” she said. “We cannot just sit back and say somebody else is going to do it.”</p><p>In order to focus on her goals, Chaz has given more responsibilities to Smith-Evans, but her daughter doesn’t expect her mother to ever fully step back.</p><p>“Sometimes people say to her, ‘Boy, you're doing a great job keeping [Roger’s] legacy going,’” said Smith-Evans, of the South Loop, who praised her mother and late stepfather as strong, compassionate and giving leaders.</p><p>“But I think it's both of their legacies. She has taken what they started and really built on that.”</p>

entries.title: Contracting firm shares in $1 billion no-bid O'Hare deal, then its executives donate to Johnson’s campaign
entries.summary: <p>In July, Mayor Brandon Johnson’s administration awarded a no-bid contract worth up to $1 billion to a clout-heavy consortium to run and maintain the "People Mover" — the automated transit system at O’Hare Airport linking the parking lots, terminals and rental car complex.</p><p>In October, four executives at Plainfield-based Harbour Contractors, Inc., each gave Friends of Brandon Johnson, the mayor's campaign fund, $2,500, for a total of $10,000, records show.</p><p>It appears to be the first time anyone from that company gave to Johnson's political account.</p><p>Harbour is part of O’Hare Airport Transit Systems, Inc., or OATS, the venture that inked the lucrative "sole source" deal with City Hall in the summer.</p><p>In 2011, then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel signed an executive order banning City Hall contractors from giving campaign money to Chicago’s mayor — a rule still in effect, meaning the Harbour donations appear to violate city ethics regulations.</p><p>Emanuel's order says "any contract negotiated, entered into, or performed in violation of any of the provisions of this order shall be terminable by the city."</p><p>It seems unlikely City Hall would pursue that. A Johnson aide said it's too early to discuss potential outcomes. </p><p>Since Johnson’s 2023 election, the Chicago Sun-Times has reported on a number of instances where that prohibition was violated by his campaign, which then returned campaign money to donors.</p><p>Johnson’s campaign spokesman Christian Perry said that’s what will happen here if it turns out Friends of Brandon Johnson shouldn't have taken the Harbour contributions.</p><p>It remains unclear how the contributions came about, including whether they were solicited by the mayor’s political camp.</p><p>Harbour's leaders didn’t respond to requests for comment.</p><p>City disclosure records show Harbour Contractors, led by Patrick Harbour, holds a 40% stake in OATS, while R.M. Chin & Associates and Riteway-Huggins Construction, Inc., own the rest.</p><p>“The original contract with OATS dates to 1994,” a city spokesman said, adding the venture is also known as AOR Transit. The Chicago Department of Aviation, or CDA, the arm of City Hall overseeing Chicago’s airports, “paid OATS approximately $56.3 million in 2025,” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Richard M. Daley was mayor from 1989 until 2011, when he retired. He was succeeded by Emanuel, who accepted a $1,500 campaign contribution from a top Harbour Contractors executive before he was elected.</p><p>Harbour or its affiliates secured no-bid work at various times under both men. And Harbour particularly flourished under Daley, who also accepted campaign money from the company and its executives.</p><p>Under Johnson, City Hall “sought a sole-source contract with OATS to retain the specialized expertise needed to operate and maintain the system’s unique combination of original infrastructure and newer technology,” the city spokesman said.</p><p>“Changing operators could create significant operational risks and disrupt a critical connection for rental car customers and passengers.”</p><p>The contract was awarded through a different arm of City Hall, Johnson’s Department of Procurement Services, the spokesman said.</p><p>City records explained the decision to pursue the work without bidding by saying: “CDA maintains that competitive solicitation would likely produce the same outcome, with [OATS] emerging as the most qualified provider based on its extensive experience, technical capabilities, institutional knowledge, and proven performance.”</p><p>The aviation department uses “airport revenue from airline rates and charges” to pay the group to “operate and maintain the Airport Transit System,” also called the ATS or People Mover.</p><p>“The three-mile automated People Mover connects Terminals 1, 2, 3 and 5 to one another and to the O’Hare Multi-Modal Facility. The system provided 13.3 million rides for passengers and airport employees in 2025, averaging 36,500 per day.”</p><p>“Following extensive upgrades, including a new train fleet and an extension to the Multi-Modal Facility, the ATS reopened in 2021 and resumed 24/7 service in 2022.”</p><p>That project was completed late, and over cost.</p><p>Harbour Contractors also is “a subcontractor to Plote Construction Inc. and to the construction management joint venture AECOM Hunt Clayco Bowa, providing survey work in support of taxiway and passenger facility construction at O'Hare,” the city spokesman said.</p><p>In November 2023, roughly six months after Johnson took office, the Sun-Times reported that his campaign fund had accepted contributions from city contractors that included a trucking company executive whose businesses have done work for City Hall, along with the operator of a janitorial business with a City Hall contract for maintenance.</p><p>The campaign fund also may have improperly accepted money from city lobbyists.</p><p>The campaign later refunded around $50,000 to donors.</p><p>Johnson’s campaign has also accepted millions of dollars from labor unions that entries.title: Construction begins on $917 million concourse at O'Hare's Terminal 2
entries.summary: <p>City and airline officials released new images Tuesday of O'Hare Airport's latest scheduled arrival: a $917 million concourse that will add natural lighting, wood details, interior greenery and, ultimately, 24 new gates to the nation's third-busiest airport.</p><p>Renderings of the new Concourse E at Terminal 2 were made public during a groundbreaking ceremony at the airport.</p><p>The event heralded the start of the concourse's $640 million initial construction phase, which is expected to be completed in 2030 and bring online 14 new gates.</p><p>A second and final phase will add 10 more gates, and the completed concourse will open in 2034.</p><p>"We are building the modern facilities necessary to keep millions of passengers moving ... for generations to come," Mayor Brandon Johnson said in a statement issued before the groundbreaking.</p><p>Johnson was joined by executives from United and American airlines — the concourse's two major users — as well as project officials.</p><p>Renderings show the concourse as a long, lozenge-shaped, curved-roofed, glassy-sided facility with skylights, soft artificial illumination, acoustic absorbent materials, the liberal use of wood paneling and surfaces — even trees and plants.</p><p>Sleek-looking retail, restaurant and lounge spaces are also planned. And in a nod to the airport site's origins as an orchard, interior support columns resemble trees.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure entries.title: Is Josh Giddey playing himself out of the Bulls' starting point guard?
entries.summary: <p>CLEVELAND – It was a no-explanation-needed moment for Josh Giddey.</p><p>As the Bulls starting guard sat most of crunch time of the fourth quarter Monday night, not one coach – including head coach Tiago Splitter – needed to stroll over and let him know why.</p><p>“Nah, I don’t need one at all,” Giddey said, referring to a heart-to-heart over the decision to bench him in the loss. “I would have done the same thing if I was Tiago. I’m not like sitting there confused by why I wasn’t playing down the stretch. It was his call, the right call. If I want to play down the stretch I’ve got to play a little better than that.”</p><p>Giddey wasn’t lying.</p><p>In his world, a 1-for-5 shooting night is bad enough. But a six-turnover game in just 24 minutes of work? Unacceptable.</p><p>Especially after Giddey was coming off a win in Minnesota in which he didn’t shoot well but handed out five assists with just one turnover.</p><p>But that’s the ongoing issue with the six-year veteran: Consistency. Yes, teams have been picking him up further up the court to try and seduce him into a turnover and get the transition game going, and with good reason.</p><p>Giddey had a four-game stretch in late October in which he totaled five turnovers. In a loss to the Spurs last week, he had seven, and then the debacle in Cleveland.</p><p>“I mean yeah, but I’m a point guard; that shouldn’t bother me,” Giddey said of the pressure opposing teams have been putting on him. “It’s bad when we’re turning the ball over as much as we are and I’m the main culprit of it, so I’ve obviously got to get better there.</p><p>“That’s a point guard’s job. If I can’t do that, I probably shouldn’t be a point guard.”</p><p>Which raised a question: Should he stay the starting Bulls point guard with backup Tre Jones playing so well?</p><p>Jones will enter Wednesday’s game in Brooklyn averaging just under 20 minutes per game, averaging 10.9 points and 1.3 turnovers per game. In just over 28 minutes of work per game, Giddey was averaging 9.9 points and 3.3 turnovers. He averaged 3.6 turnovers per game last season for Billy Donovan.</p><p>The armchair overreactors would say make the switch. Splitter isn’t that.</p><p>The coach was asked if he was thinking about making a change and if there was a set number of games he needed in order to validate that decision.</p><p>“I don’t have a set number, no,” Splitter said. “I think it’s more like a feel to be honest. But you mentioned Tre and Josh, and I think they’ve played some games, some minutes (together). Not as much. You’re also going to lose some shooting in those units.</p><p>“You can’t just try everything, it’s hard to try everything. We could play double bigs, we could play three shooters on the court, play two point guards, so there’s a lot of things you can do differently. Right now, I always feel like I have to play bigger to rebound the ball better and win those possessions. Yes, we try, we have a feel, and we have a sample size we look at, and go from there.”</p><p>That’s the key with Giddey and why he does have value with the group, especially now. Caleb Wilson is sidelined with hand surgery, and Nic Claxton is still on a minutes restriction. Giddey is 6-foot-7 and is coming off a 2025-26 campaign in which he averaged a career-high 8.3 rebounds per game.</p><p>He just needs to play a cleaner brand of basketball.</p><p>“Such a crucial thing with possessions these days,” Giddey added. “The more we turn the ball over the less possessions we have. Turnovers are just killing us and I’m killing us with those.”</p>

entries.title: Police on scene of bomb threat at Jones College Prep
entries.summary: <p>Chicago police are on the scene at Jones College Prep high school Tuesday morning in the Loop investigating a bomb threat, according to police and a witness. </p><p>No one has been injured and police remain on the scene of the school 700 S. State St. as of 8 a.m., a police spokesperson said.</p><p>Chicago Fire firefighters have not been called to the scene, according to a spokesperson. </p><p>Students have been moved to the South Loop elementary school, 1212 S. Plymouth Ct., according to a witness, who added police were bringing dogs into the school after the threat, which was received from a voicemail. </p><p>As of about 8:10 a.m., police were sweeping the building and focusing on a U-Haul vehicle which had been left near the school for a day or so, according to the witness. </p><p>CPS had no information. </p><p><i>This is a developing story. Check back for details. </i><br></p>

Mitchell</a></h5><p><b>Conviction tossed</b>: A Cook County judge on Monday threw out the conviction of Anthony Garrett, 68, finding that his written confession in 7-year-old Dantrell Davis' 1992 murder was likely tortured out of him.</p><p><b>The ruling</b>: The judge's written order made it clear she didn't buy sworn testimony from Richard Zuley, 80, a retired Chicago detective accused of orchestrating Garrett's alleged beating in custody after the fatal shooting. The judge ordered a retrial and Garrett's transfer from an Illinois prison to Cook County Jail.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: Davis was fatally shot as he walked to school with his mother in the former public housing complex Cabrini-Green. Garrett, convicted by a jury in 1994, was sentenced to 100 years in prison. Before his conviction was tossed Monday, Garrett's attorney tied his alleged torture to <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-m/" target="_blank" >Zuley-led coercion</a> in a string of cases from 1987 to 2003 — including four murder convictions later thrown out.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-c/"
