</div> </div><p></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-ju/" target="_blank" >Chaz Ebert carries Roger’s legacy – and walks her own path</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-tl/" target="_blank" >Erica Thompson</a></h5><p>Chaz Ebert is still in love with the movies.</p><p>One of the first to arrive at the Chicago International Film Festival this year, she remained a constant presence, winding through crowds and taking in several screenings she said inspired her to continue efforts and conversations she used to share with her late husband, famed Sun-Times film critic Roger Ebert.</p><p>Chaz oversees several enterprises in honor of her late spouse. That includes the Roger and Chaz Ebert Foundation and the criticism website <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-tr/" target="_blank" >rogerebert.com</a>.</p><p>She spends her days approving projects, such as the fundraising campaign for a life-sized, bronze sculpture of Ebert's iconic partner-in-criticism, Gene Siskel. There is also a documentary, play and biopic in the works about the friends — and sometimes foes — who taped their first TV review show more than 50 years ago.</p><p>But Chaz is also leaning into her own creative and charitable pursuits. In recent years, she has directed a short documentary, penned a book, and in 2027, she will host an event honoring inspirational leaders. And she helps fund the Chicago International Film Festival's Black Perspectives program celebrating films by African Americans and those throughout the African diaspora. She's also writing a musical about the Virgin Mary.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydkletl-l-ty/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>PICTURE entries.title: White Sox add free-agent right-hander Dustin May to bolster starting rotation
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox are not done adding former Milwaukee Brewers this offseason, but this signing might get more attention than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/29/white-sox-hiring-matt-roffe-away-from-brewers-to-fill-open-amateur-scouting-director-role" target="_blank" ><u>a new amateur scouting director</u></a>.</p><p>A source confirmed to the Sun-Times that the Sox are signing 29-year-old right-hander Dustin May to a three-year, $52.5 million contract, following their strongly stated need to add starting pitching this winter. May has cleared over 130 innings each of the past two seasons, after injuries slowed the early portions of a career that began as a revered Dodgers pitching prospect.</p><p>Averaging nearly 97 mph with his fastball and generating above-average extension off the mound, the six-foot-six May is still a physical marvel who displays the tools that made him a consensus top-25 prospect in the sport ahead of the 2020 season. Confoundingly for a man who is set to receive the largest free-agent outlay the White Sox have extended in the last four years, the on-field results have lagged behind.</p><p>After missing the 2024 season recovering from Tommy John surgery revision and an esophageal tear, May has posted a 4.85 ERA over the past two years; split across four teams since he’s been dealt midseason two trade deadlines in a row. This August, May was dealt to the Brewers and stayed in their rotation throughout their World Series run, but undeniably struggled. He recorded a 5.65 ERA in 36 ⅔ innings during the regular season after the trade, and allowed seven earned runs in 11 innings of postseason work, including a memorable three-run homer he yielded to Shohei Ohtani in the National League Championship Series.</p><p>May has allowed a .801 OPS to left-handed hitters over the past two seasons, and developing a better off-speed weapon to go alongside his breaking ball-heavy profile is a likely target area for White Sox pitching coaches. Many advanced metrics–and inevitably the Sox’ internal numbers–are far more bullish on the strength of May’s arsenal and command than his results would indicate. In that vein, the right-hander offers the opportunity for a budget-conscious Sox team to land someone with the talent of a mid-rotation starter, at a price discounted by the absence of an above-average full season on his resume.</p><p>But to complete that sort of a coup, the White Sox will have to succeed in getting standout surface-level results out of May where other organizations respected for their pitching development–Brewers, Dodgers, Red Sox–have failed.</p><p>Both Dallas Keuchel ($55.5 million) and Liam Hendriks ($54 million) received slightly higher guarantees, so May will become the owner of the third-largest free-agent contract for a pitcher in White Sox history. He will join a rotation currently heavy on projects and bounce-back candidates behind staff ace Sean Burke. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/11/that-suckers-built-different-grant-taylors-move-to-white-sox-rotation-fits-his-boundary-pushing-style" target="_blank" ><u>Grant Taylor is trying to pull off a conversion</u></a> from relieving last season, Davis Martin is trying to shake off a poor second half worsened by a right calf issue, and Luis Castillo will be trying to redeem the final season of an even larger contract after a career-worst 2026 season.</p><p>If Sox’ run prevention takes the step forward in 2027 that their offense managed in 2026, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/18/white-sox-noah-schultz-hagen-smith-tanner-mcdougal-david-sandlin-brian-bannister-will-venable-erick-fedde-jose-urquidy-davis-martin-al-central" target="_blank" ><u>their pitching development</u></a> will need to carry the day.</p>

entries.title: Downtown and Near North Side District 6a Chicago School Board race too close to call
entries.summary:
District 6a neighborhoods: Near North Side, West Town

The candidate supported by a billionaire-backed political group and charter proponents continued to have a narrow lead over two progressives as of Tuesday, Nov. 17 but the race was too close to call.

With all precincts reporting, around 100 votes separated Isaiah White, a school support worker from Anusha Thotakura, the incumbent who runs a statewide advocacy organization, according to Chicago Board of Election results. Meanwhile, Brenda Lee Anderson, a Northwestern University lecturer on leave, trailed White by just under 1,200 votes.

Election officials have until Nov. 17 to finish counting mail-in ballots and provisional ballots. Final official results are due on Nov. 24.

White said his analysis showed that mail-in ballots historically haven't diverged more than 1% from the pattern of other ballots, which could keep him in the lead. "So, we are cautiously optimistic we will hold our lead, but not taking anything for granted," he said earlier this month. "We are taking everything seriously."

The close race was somewhat unexpected. Voters in the area typically support more conservative candidates. But across the city, candidates supported by the Chicago Teachers Union are doing better than expected after being significantly outspent.

Thotakura got support from the CTU and the Service Employees International Union, which represents school support workers. She seems to be splitting the more left-leaning vote with Anderson, who was not backed by any special interests.

More than $500,000 was spent on White’s campaign by The Urban Center, a centrist political organization that advocates for school choice across public and private schools, and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools. He also was endorsed by an anti-CTU political action committee that is heavily funded by billionaire Michael Sacks and says it aims to engage voters around “effective progressive policies.”

Given its location as part of the commercial and business center of the city, District 6a has just 14 public schools — the fewest of any school board electoral districts — and none are neighborhood high schools. The students who attend Chicago Public Schools here include a more diverse mix than in most districts, but the schools have more white and Asian American students than CPS as a whole.

Two of the schools in the district have the highest rating given by the state; while 60% had the lowest two distinctions, “developing” and “comprehensive,” according to 2026 state data released last week. There are now six levels of designations, up from the five up last year when the bottom two were called “comprehensive” and “intensive.”

Thotakura’s and White’s main priorities are to boost reading and math scores. Anderson’s main goal is to fix CPS’ chronic budget crisis.

Contributing: Reema Amin, Chalkbeat Chicago and Kate Grossman

entries.title: US loses measles elimination status as cases remain low in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>In 2000, the United States was able to officially declare measles eliminated in the country, a hard-fought victory in public health. Twenty six years later, the U.S. can no longer make that claim. </p><p>After years of rising anti-vaccine rhetoric and anti-public health sentiments, the U.S. has suffered several large measles outbreaks. And on Tuesday, a global panel of health experts formally determined that the country has lost "measles elimination status" — meaning the U.S. has gone more than 12 months with uninterrupted transmission of measles. </p><p>"This reflects a complacency that has grown in the last couple decades because people don't see the severity of measles on a day-to-day basis," said Dr. Ravi Jhaveri, the division head of pediatric infectious diseases at Lurie Children’s Hospital.</p><p>"No one should be dying of measles in the U.S.," Jhaveri said. "Not a single person." </p><p>A committee of the Pan American Health Organization, a branch of the World Health Organization, announced their long-anticipated decision Tuesday morning. Mexico also lost its status. </p><p>“Measles elimination is not a trophy that is won once and placed on a shelf,” said Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO’s director. “It is an achievement that must be safeguarded every day by closing immunity gaps and ensuring we reach every community.”</p><p>Measles is a highly contagious virus that starts with a high fever followed by a rash. Most people are able to recover, but it's one of the leading causes of death among young children, according to the World Health Organization.</p><p>The last two years have been among the worst for measles in the U.S. with more than 7,000 cases and 11 deaths. Most of the people infected were either unvaccinated or didn't share if they'd had the vaccine. </p><p>While outbreaks have pummeled several states, Illinois continues to see a low count of measles cases. So far in 2026, <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/diseases-and-conditions/measles.html" target="_blank" >29 cases have been reported</a> to the Illinois Department of Public Health. No one has died from the virus or been hospitalized this year. Cook County has only one reported case so far this year. Downstate Douglas County has reported the most with 11 cases.</p><p>But in previous years, Illinois has reported single-digit case counts or no cases at all.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-3d0000" name="html-embed-module-3d0000"></a><div style="min-height:438px" id="datawrapper-vis-rL1ub"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/rL1ub/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-rL1ub"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/rL1ub/full.png" alt="Number of measles cases per year in Illinois (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Over 5,700 cases have been reported nationwide in 2026, according to <a class="Link" href="https://publichealth.jhu.edu/ivac/resources/us-measles-tracker" target="_blank" >state and county health department data compiled by Johns Hopkins</a>. Over 1,500 cases have been found in Pennsylvania alone. </p><p>Illinois' rate for the two-dose measles vaccine is holding steady among school-aged children, according to data from the Illinois State Board of Education. For the 2025-2026 school year, the state's vaccination rate is 96.8%. Chicago Public Schools rate is 95.7%, an improvement after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/05/08/less-than-half-of-cps-schools-have-herd-immunity-for-measles-state-data-shows" target="_blank" >district saw a dip</a> in vaccinations coming out of the COVID-19 pandemic. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d70000" name="html-embed-module-d70000"></a><div style="min-height:387px" id="datawrapper-vis-BS7QD"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BS7QD/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-BS7QD"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/BS7QD/full.png" alt="Measles vaccination rates in Illinois and Chicago Public Schools (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>A vaccination rate of 95% is a benchmark public health experts use to determine whether a community has hit "herd immunity."</p><p>Jhaveri emphasized that most parents are still getting their kids vaccinated and a "small fragment of the population" is forgoing the shot. </p><p>In the Chicago area, "we still do a great job of having most of our children get the two doses of the vaccine," Jhaveri said. "The risk for us locally is not that high. There will still be small clusters, small outbreaks." </p><p><i>Contributing: Associated Press</i> </p>

entries.title: How Jaguars-Bears in Week 13 could be flexed — or not
entries.summary: <p>Whether the NFL flexes the Bears’ game Dec. 6 against the Jaguars into prime time could depend on whether the Texans lose to the Colts on Thursday.</p><p>But there are plenty of other factors that could determine the kickoff time between teams currently 7-2, which is scheduled for noon on Fox. Here’s a breakdown:</p><p>NBC’s “Sunday Night Football” game Dec. 6 is Texans-Steelers. At 6-3, the Steelers are in playoff contention, but the Texans would drop to 3-7 with a loss to the Colts, likely knocking them out of contention. That would open the door for flexing. If the Texans win, the NFL likely would say both teams are contending and keep the game in prime time.</p><p>Some would debate the Texans’ legitimacy in that scenario, but it’s important to remember the point of flexible scheduling: It’s not to put the best game in prime time, it’s to replace a bad game with a better game. Assuming the Texans win, Texans-Steelers wouldn’t be a bad game, and its viewership might be in line with Jaguars-Bears. The Jags don’t exactly move the needle.</p><p>Plus, Jaguars-Bears isn’t the only game with a chance of being flexed in Week 13. The 49ers-Giants game, scheduled for noon on Fox, is a battle of division leaders. Same with Panthers-Vikings, which is set for 3:25 p.m. on CBS. The Bills-Patriots game, also set for 3:25 p.m. on CBS, took a hit with the injury to Pats quarterback Drake Maye.</p><p>Then the question becomes, which games do CBS and Fox protect? Would Fox protect 49ers-Giants over Jags-Bears? Probably. But Fox is guaranteed a number of Bears games each season. Could losing that game mean Bears-Dolphins in Week 14 would move from CBS to Fox? It’s possible.</p><p>It’s not like the Bears or Jaguars need another prime-time game, anyway. The Bears just had three consecutive night games, and after facing the Bears, the Jags will play in prime time in two of the next three weeks.</p><p>That said, the NFL aims to give the best distribution to its biggest games. If Jaguars-Bears stays on Fox, it likely would go to only a third of the country, in competition with 49ers-Giants and Packers-Saints. For a potential matchup of 9-2 teams, it needs more viewership.</p><p>The NFL doesn’t need to make a decision until next Tuesday, and NFL commissioner Roger Goodell has the final say. With every permutation, there’s always wiggle room to give the boss what he wants.</p>

entries.title: Tiger Woods to return to competition for first time in two years at Hero World Challenge
entries.summary: <p>Tiger Woods is returning to competition for the first time in two years, announcing Tuesday he will be playing in the Hero World Challenge at the unofficial event he hosts in the Bahamas.</p><p>His decision was posted on Instagram, with Woods joining the 20-man field along with Rickie Fowler and 2019 U.S. Open champion Gary Woodland.</p><p>The Hero World Challenge at Albany Golf Club is Dec. 3-6.</p><p>Woods last competed in the 2024 British Open at Royal Troon, where he missed the cut in his last year playing all four majors. He also played with his son at the 36-hole PNC Championship, where he could ride in a cart.</p><p>Woods ruptured his Achilles tendon in February 2025 and missed the entire year, and then had a seventh back surgery in October of that year to replace a disk in his lower back.</p><p>He was starting to practice ahead of the Masters early this year when he was arrested and jailed on a DUI charge after his SUV clipped a trailer and flipped on its side while driving down a residential road in Florida.</p><p>A sheriff's report said deputies found two pain pills in his pocket and Woods showed signs of impairment. A breath test was negative, but he refused a urine test.</p><p>Woods left the country to seek treatment, and in September he pleaded no contest to a reckless driving charge. His driver's license was suspended for five years.</p><p>The 20-man field in Nassau is for players from the top 50 in the world ranking, though it reserves a spot for the tournament host. It is sanctioned by the PGA Tour and offers world ranking points.</p><p>For Woods, it will be his first time walking 72 holes since he set a Masters record in 2024 by making the cut for the 24th consecutive time. He missed the cut in the other three majors.</p><p>Woods, with 15 majors and a record-tying 82 victories on the PGA Tour, has not won since the Zozo Championship in Japan in October 2019.</p><p>Of all the injuries to his left knee and lower back, none was more devastating than those he suffered in the 2021 car crash when he was driving at a high rate of speed and rolled his SUV down a hill outside of Los Angeles. His right leg and ankle were so badly mangled that Woods said doctors contemplated amputation.</p><p>But he returned a year later at the Masters. While the 50-year-old Woods still swings well, he has not finished closer than 16 shots of the winning score in the 10 times he has played since the car crash, including one year against the 20-man field in the Bahamas.</p><p>Woods just completed his work as chairman of the Future Competition Committee on the PGA Tour that has reshaped the competition model for 2028.<br></p>

entries.title: Michael O'Brien's preseason Super 25 Illinois high school basketball rankings
entries.summary: <p>Top-ranked Neuqua Valley does not want to be a two-man show this season, despite how fun that show was to watch last season. Dynamic junior Cole Kelly and Illinois recruit Mason Martin are tall, athletic players with seemingly unlimited shooting range.</p><p>Both players averaged 20 points last year and overwhelmed most teams with their firepower. But that is not the plan for the Wildcats this winter.</p><p>“We hate the two-man show,” Neuqua Valley coach Todd Sutton said. “That is where we started seeing the triangle and two [defense] last year. And that was a problem.”</p><p>Glenbrook North’s 2005 state championship team, led by Jon Scheyer and Sean Wallis, is the best historical comparison for the Wildcats. Scheyer was one of the best players in Illinois history, but the team won due to incredible chemistry and preparation. They couldn't match up talent-wise against the other state powers.</p><p>Neuqua Valley hasn’t shown that level of cohesion yet, but it is the goal.</p><h3>1. Neuqua Valley</h3><p>Kelly and Martin are a year more experienced, as is the supporting cast. Luke Balgro, Carter Coviello and Arshil Khimani won’t be overwhelmed by big-game atmospheres. A lot depends on 6-2 Danny Mikuta and 6-4 Hunter Rheaume, undersized bigs who will be tested often. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/2026/11/16/neuqua-valley-basketball-cole-kelly-mason-martin" >Read more on Neuqua Valley.</a></p><h3>2. Benet</h3><p>Starting forwards Ed Stasys (Yale) and Perry Tchienge return, and senior guards Blair Fagbemi and Tyler Cibulka will have much larger roles. Cormac Hanus, a 6-5 senior, and 6-5 junior Brandon Otten showed promise over the summer.</p><h3>3. Evanston</h3><p>Possibly the strongest returning core in the state with 6-5 Vito Rocca (Dartmouth), 6-5 Tate Schroeder, junior guard Ben Ojala and senior Dion Lane. The best offensive team in school history last season, the focus will be on improving the defense.</p><h3>4. Bolingbrook</h3><p>The new group is deep and talented, led by junior Brady Pettigrew, the state’s top prospect. Senior Nate Woods, an excellent shooter, transferred from Lyons. Six-foot-five junior Dereon Smothers joined from Butler and 6-6 Curtis Stubbs from Providence. Isaiah Rogers, a 6-4 senior, returns with brothers Mason and Marlon Williams. Freshman Layton Jones will contribute.</p><h3>5. East St. Louis</h3><p>Senior Phillip Jones will be one of the state’s best scorers. Starters Terri’yon Webster and Tyrik Barnes also return. Sophomore Emurion Jackson, a 6-5 combo guard, is one of the state’s top prospects.</p><h3>6. St. Laurence</h3><p>One of the state’s deepest rosters, led by senior UIC recruit Markese Peoples. Logan Brown, a 6-5 junior, is poised for a breakout season. Jeremiah Toney and Noah Corro are back, and there are big expectations for sophomores Evan Lemons and Lawrence Burnett. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-basketball/2026/11/09/first-day-of-practice-is-a-new-basketball-powerhouse-under-construction-at-st-laurence" >Read more on St. Laurence.</a></p><h3>7. St. Ignatius</h3><p>One of the state’s best shooting teams. Junior Amir Tucker emerged as a go-to guard last season. Duke Ross, a 6-5 senior, returns along with DJ Caldwell and Chris Chittaro. Another deep roster, with very talented junior and sophomore classes.</p><h3>8. Peoria Richwoods</h3><p>Junior guard Amarion Smith-Holley is one of the state’s most exciting players. Size will be the biggest issue, but 6-5 JJ Duffin transferred in from Peoria Central, and that will help. Guards Kingston Weatherspoon, Carmelo Hearn and Orlando Edwards are major pieces.</p><h3>9. Homewood-Flossmoor</h3><p>Darrius Hawkins Jr. is a force. The experienced junior point guard elevates his teammates to another level. Senior guard Danny Ruffin and 6-6 junior John Brown IV also return.</p><h3>10. Lockport</h3><p>Senior twins Nojus and Nedas Venckus (Emporia State) are talented all-around scorers, and Nathan Munson is a rock-solid point guard. Grady Ruane also returns, and newcomers Jayde Wyett and Elias Passehl will be major contributors.</p><h3>11. Centralia</h3><p>Talented multi-sport athletes Archie Goewey and Kenny Bratton, both juniors, return from a 32-2 squad last season. Lee Bennett is considered one of the state’s best coaches. The Orphans are one of the winningest programs in the country, with more than 2,400 victories.</p><h3>12. Oswego</h3><p>Junior guard Ethan Vahl is an electric player, and 6-10 Cole Jansons continues to improve. Graham Schwab and MJ Johnson also return. Brothers Tray and Jayden Alford, transfers from Yorkville Christian, add scoring punch.</p><h3>13. Leo</h3><p>Nearly the entire roster is back from last season’s team, which finished fourth in 3A. Guards Karon Shavers, Brian Kizer, Jeremiah Echols, Asa Harris and Kierre Brooks are experienced, and 6-10 sophomore Elon Henderson is one of the state’s intriguing prospects.</p><h3>14. Metamora</h3><p>A big two-year run starts now. Starters Sam Koch, Brady Jones, Briggs Bucy and Logan Vasquez return. Six-foot-seven junior Cam Beekman is receiving college interest.</p><h3>15. Belleville West</h3><p>Missouri State recruit J’dyn Lloyd, a 6-5 senior, is one of the state’s top players. Senior TJ Cason also returns. A gifted, athletic team with size.</p><h3>16. Kenwood</h3><p>Seniors Damari Stephens and Osiris Bell provide a solid, experienced foundation. There are high hopes for 6-8 junior Elijah Shim and freshman guard Elijah McKinnie.</p><h3>17. Perspectives-Leadership</h3><p>Senior Michael Woods returns to the city after a couple of years in Indiana. He’s expected to be one of the state’s best guards. Starting guard Jayden Taylor is back, and 6-8 Joshua Hinton, another transfer from Indiana, will be a huge factor.</p><h3>18. Peoria Central</h3><p>Guards Kayden Turner and Nigel Moore had excellent offseasons and are among the state's top 20 juniors. Sophomore Danny Ruffin impressed last season, and 6-6 senior Cyrow Childs is an impact rebounder.</p><h3>19. DePaul Prep</h3><p>There’s a lot to replace, but junior Blake Choice and 6-8 Gus Johnson return. Junior guard Jacob Only transferred in from St. Viator and will provide solid scoring.</p><h3>20. Glenbrook North</h3><p>Point guard Nate Fridman, junior guard Charlie Lappin and junior forward Mason Markman return from the starting lineup. Irakli Kipiani, a 6-7 junior, will have an expanded role and keep an eye on 6-6 center Isaac Moser.</p><h3>21. King</h3><p>The team has a solid core in Corey Wellere Jr., Terrel Keys, and JaKobe Wren. Junior guard Jacob Wren is poised for a breakout season. Two major transfer additions put the Jaguars over the top: DK Heard, one of the state’s best sophomores, and junior guard Roosevelt Thomas.</p><h3>22. Marist</h3><p>Only one starter, Kendall Meyers, is back from the 4A championship team. MJ Greene and Jayden Bullock contributed last season, and 6-5 Caden Crudup, a Young transfer, will add some size and experience. Juniors JJ Nash and Jaylen Francis are in the mix, along with highly touted freshman Robert Smith Jr.</p><h3><b>23. Bloom</b></h3><p>The sophomore backcourt of Keiwon Gulley and Kaden McClellan should be among the state’s best. Junior guard Lester Watson transferred in after a big year at Thornwood, and freshman Larry Ellis arrives on a wave of hype with 6-8 freshman Louis Johnson.</p><h3>24. Glenbard North</h3><p>New coach Nick Healy has two of the state’s best seniors in guard Lamari Carpenter and 6-5 Oturo Redento. Senior Caeden Chilton and junior George Schager are experienced and improved over the summer.</p><h3>25. Curie</h3><p>Can coach Mike Oliver do it again? Only Tobyus Banks returns from last season, but the new group went 28-0 and won the city as sophomores. Dream Horton, Malik Horton, and 6-6 junior Amir Green will make an immediate impact, and sophomore Theonte Robinson has potential.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-430000" name="html-embed-module-430000"></a><iframe title="No Shot Clock, Ep. 207: Revealing the 2026-27 statewide preseason Super 25 rankings" allowtransparency="true" height="150" width="100%" style="border: none; min-width: min(100%, 430px);height:150px;" scrolling="no" data-name="pb-iframe-player" src="https://www.podbean.com/player-v2/?i=u6iwm-1bb41bc-pb&from=pb6admin&share=1&download=1&rtl=0&fonts=Arial&skin=1&font-color=auto&logo_link=episode_page&btn-skin=c73a3a" loading="lazy"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: 50 personas prestan juramento de ciudadanía estadounidense en el museo mexicano de Pilsen
entries.summary: <p>Tras recitar el Juramento de Lealtad el lunes por la mañana, el nuevo ciudadano estadounidense Roberto Flores permaneció en el Museo Nacional de Arte Mexicano con su prometida para recorrer las salas.</p><p>Para Flores, de 49 años, la ceremonia tuvo un significado especial. Llegó a Estados Unidos desde Michoacán cuando tenía 2 años. Creció en Pilsen y La Villita y había tenido la residencia desde 1990.</p><p>“Es algo grandioso lo que están haciendo aquí”, dijo Flores. “También estoy orgulloso de ser mexicano, ahora que soy estadounidense”.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a70000" name="module-a70000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Flores estuvo entre 50 personas de 24 países que se convirtieron en ciudadanos el lunes en el museo. Entre ellos, 16 eran de México, según la Corte de Distrito de Estados Unidos para el Distrito Norte de Illinois. La jueza principal de la Corte de Distrito, Virginia M. Kendall, presidió la ceremonia y administró el juramento.</p><p>Fue la primera vez que el museo, que tiene 44 años, celebró una ceremonia de naturalización.</p><div class="Enhancement" lunes tras convertirse en ciudadano de Estados Unidos. Flores fue uno de los 50 participantes que prestaron el juramento de lealtad durante la ceremonia de naturalización celebrada en el museo. Nació en Michoacán, México, y fue traído a Estados Unidos por su abuela cuando tenía dos años.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>El museo, en 1852 W. 19th St., fue fundado por educadores que buscaban ayudar a los jóvenes mexicoamericanos a mantenerse conectados con sus raíces culturales, dijo José Ochoa, presidente y director ejecutivo del museo. Se concibió como un lugar donde los inmigrantes pudieran construir una vida en Estados Unidos sin perder el vínculo con su herencia.</p><p>“Podemos seguir siendo de donde venimos. Y también podemos ser de aquí”, dijo Ochoa a los nuevos ciudadanos.</p><p>Para Rosario Lara, de 73 años, que vive en Brighton Park, la ciudadanía significó una oportunidad para participar más plenamente en su comunidad. Originaria de la Ciudad de México, Lara dijo que había sido residente permanente durante 16 años antes de convertirse en ciudadana.</p><p>“Quiero servir a mi comunidad y quiero votar”, dijo, a través de un familiar que ayudó a traducir.</p><p>Al igual que Flores, el representante estadounidense Jesús “Chuy” García, que se retira, también emigró de México siendo niño. Cuando García se dirigió a los nuevos ciudadanos, recordó haber llegado al vecindario en 1965 con su madre y sus hermanos.</p><p>“Nunca olvidemos que esta nación fue construida por inmigrantes”, dijo entries.title: Charges filed after intruder eludes dorm security, grabs student by throat at Northwestern University
entries.summary: <p>A man who sneaked into a Northwestern University dormitory, evaded layers of security and followed a student into her room where he grabbed her by the throat Sunday was arrested soon after and remains behind bars, police said. </p><p>Diaunte E. Adams, 23, is charged with aggravated battery/strangle, criminal trespassing and home invasion causing injury, court records show. Adams was scheduled for a detention hearing Tuesday at the Old Orchard Courthouse in Skokie.</p><p>Classmates who rushed to assist the student are being credited with helping her escape after the attack late Sunday afternoon, according to Northwestern University Police.</p><p>According to court records, Adams had followed two students from the Noyes Street station on the CTA Purple Line to Elder Hall, 2400 Sheridan Road on the northern part of the Northwestern campus. Adams, who is not affiliated with the university, then followed a student into Elder Hall through an open door, according to Northwestern police. Once inside, he allegedly bypassed two more layers of security by "tailgating" — following close behind students — through secured areas.</p><p>He then gained access to the fourth-floor elevator and proceeded down the hall, where he followed another student into her room about 5 p.m.</p><p>“Upon turning around, she observed Adams standing in her room, staring at her,” records show.</p><p>When she tried to flee, she was able to open the door only part way, and Adams grabbed her and began choking her, records show. During the struggle, he injured her leg as she kept the door ajar with her left foot while calling for help, records show.</p><p>Another student who heard the commotion tried to push Adams away, but couldn't, so she ran for help, records show. That's when several more people freed her from Adams’ chokehold and held the door closed to prevent him from leaving until Northwestern police arrived.</p><p>The student who was attacked was treated at a nearby hospital and released, police said. </p><p>Adams was placed into custody after Evanston police were called when he refused to come out of the room, records show. Adams, of Chicago Heights, later surrendered. </p><p>“Northwestern is grateful for the courage of the students who stepped in to help a fellow student,” the university said in a statement. “Personal safety is a shared responsibility, whether on campus or elsewhere. We encourage members of our community to be aware of their surroundings and report suspicious activities to local law enforcement.”</p><p>The university said security in the area has been increased.</p>

entries.title: UChicago rarely expels students found responsible for sexual assault, records show
entries.summary: <p>The University of Chicago rarely expels students who commit sexual assault, a WBEZ analysis of nearly two decades of school records shows, leaving the door open for most survivors to come face-to-face with their attackers on campus.</p><p>Between 2007 and 2025, the university expelled just seven out of 36 students that a disciplinary committee determined had committed sexual assault, <a class="Link" href="https://studentmanual.uchicago.edu/disciplinary-reports/" target="_blank" ><u>according to UChicago reports</u></a> detailing whether students were found responsible for sexual misconduct and, if so, how they were disciplined.</p><p>Nineteen sexual assaults were punished with suspension, with some students allowed to return to campus in as little as nine weeks, reports show. In the other 10 cases, students who committed sexual assault were put on probation or given a warning.</p><p>Scrutiny of how universities hold students accountable for sexual violence has intensified following an alleged gang rape at Cornell University. The university accused two of seven students involved of sexual assault, according to The New York Times, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.cornellsun.com/article/2026/10/records-reveal-cornell-s-punishments-for-seven-chi-phi-defendants" target="_blank" ><u>both were expelled</u></a>. The other five were suspended, put on probation, or given writing assignments.</p><p>Following <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/21/university-chicago-sexual-assault" target="_blank" ><u>two recent reports</u></a> of sexual assaults with ties to the University of Chicago, students there want college officials to establish <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/news/2026/10/28/university-of-chicago-students-rally-with-jane-doe-in-wake-of-sexual-assault-reports" target="_blank" ><u>more stringent minimum sanctions</u></a> for sexual violence.</p><p>“Universities remove students for plagiarism,” said Nicole Bedera, a sociologist who studies campus sexual assault and wrote the book “On The Wrong Side: How Universities Protect Perpetrators and Betray Survivors of Sexual Violence.” “That's not illegal. That is not a crime. That is just a norm that they have set.”</p><p>Bedera said many universities, not just UChicago, allow students who have committed sexual assault to stay in school and graduate. In New York, where state law requires universities to report how sexual misconduct is disciplined, 11 campuses that enroll at least 10,000 students on average per year <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/nation/2026/10/13/cornell-colleges-rape-expel-graphics-data/92172578007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p" target="_blank" ><u>did not expel a single student</u></a> for sexual violence from 2018 to 2024, according to reporting by USA Today.</p><p>“We're asking our schools right now: ‘Why is this not a norm that you care about?’” Bedera said. “Why are you happy to have the name of your institution on the diploma of a violent person?”</p><p>Most students do not report their sexual assaults to college officials, according to a 2020 report based on survey data collected by the <a class="Link" href="https://www.aau.edu/uploads/images/general/Revised-Aggregate-report-and-appendices-1-7_01-16-2020_FINAL.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Association of American Universities</u></a>.</p><p>At UChicago, when students do report an assault, an associate dean reviews information from the survivor and alleged perpetrator and either dismisses the complaint, works with the two sides to resolve the complaint administratively or refers it to a discipline committee made up of students, staff and professors from across the university.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/ILCS/Articles?ActID=1080&ChapterID=18" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois law requires</u></a> colleges to report to the attorney general how many students are suspended, expelled or otherwise disciplined for violations of sexual misconduct policies. At UChicago, the faculty senate also requests this data, and the university maintains <a class="Link" href="https://studentmanual.uchicago.edu/disciplinary-reports/" target="_blank" ><u>more detailed annual reports</u></a> about the discipline committee’s decisions online. But the reports do not explain why students found responsible for sexual assault are or are not expelled.</p><p>UChicago spokesperson Gerald McSwiggan said in a written statement that the university takes reports of sexual misconduct “extremely seriously, with care and support for victims,” and that members of the university-wide disciplinary committee are trained on the school’s harassment, discrimination and sexual misconduct policy.</p><p>“Because the policy covers a wide range of sexual misconduct, the committee carefully determines sanctions on a case-by-case basis after a thorough review of the nature and severity of the conduct involved,” McSwiggan wrote.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Students rallied in support of sexual assault victims on the quad at the University of Chicago in late October following reports of two assaults tied to the university.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Many survivors leave college after reporting sexual assault </b></h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://d3qi0qp55mx5f5.cloudfront.net/studentmanual/i/basic_pages/University_Disciplinary_Actions_2023-2024.pdf?mtime=1739226731" target="_blank" ><u>During the 2023-24 school year</u></a>, UChicago’s disciplinary committee determined a graduate student who’d been accused of sexual assault was responsible for drugging and videotaping someone engaged in sexual activity while they were unconscious. Committee members put the graduate student on probation and banned them from holding student leadership positions.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://d3qi0qp55mx5f5.cloudfront.net/studentmanual/i/basic_pages/Student_Disciplinary_Actions_2021-22_Final.pdf?mtime=1682531262" target="_blank" >In November 2021</a>, a student found responsible for sexually assaulting and sexually abusing another UChicago student was issued a three-quarter suspension. Later that month, the discipline committee found the student responsible for two more sexual assaults and expelled the student.</p><p>“The perpetrators of sexual violence in those spaces are on a fast track to be in control of our social institutions moving forward,” Bedera said. “If this is how they're taught to seek power and privilege, if this is where they are taught impunity — that is a lesson that follows them after they graduate.”</p><p>There is a lesson that follows survivors too, researchers and advocates say.</p><p>Christina Zuba, an attorney with the Chicago Alliance Against Sexual Exploitation who supports survivors through campus sexual assault investigations, said her clients often ask themselves: “Can I stay if I lose my case, and can I stay if I win my case and he's not removed from campus?”</p><p>Many decide to leave, she said.</p><p>That’s true nationally. <a class="Link" href="https://www.advocatesforyouth.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Know-Your-IX-2021-Cost-of-Reporting.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Two in five survivors</u></a> surveyed in 2020 by the advocacy group Know Your IX took a leave of absence, transferred or dropped out of school after reporting their assaults to college officials.</p><p>Survivors who stay in college often battle mental health challenges and struggle to go to class and focus on their studies, according to the 2020 survey data from the <a class="Link" href="https://www.aau.edu/uploads/images/general/Revised-Aggregate-report-and-appendices-1-7_01-16-2020_FINAL.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>Association of American Universities</u></a>.</p><p>Zuba said colleges and universities need to do more to support students through these challenges and to keep them safe.</p><p>“If a person wants to continue on at that school to reclaim their life, or to refuse to have their life further upended or damaged by the harm another person caused to them, they should be able to do that,” Zuba said.</p><p>For too many survivors, she said, the support they need never comes.</p><p>While many students who commit sexual assault stay in school and eventually cross the commencement stage, survivors often fear running into the person who hurt them, which, combined with the trauma caused by their attack, can derail their education, leaving them without a degree and with thousands of dollars in student debt.</p><p><i>This story was updated on Nov. 17, 2026 to provide additional details about the timing of the UChicago discipline committee’s decisions in November 2021.</i></p><p><i>Lisa Kurian Philip covers higher education for WBEZ in partnership with </i><a class="Link" href="https://www.opencampusmedia.org/" target="_blank" ><i><u>Open Campus</u></i></a><i>. </i></p>

entries.title: Bears report: WR Luther Burden clears concussion protocol
entries.summary: <p> What we learned Tuesday at Halas Hall:</p><h3>Burden cleared</h3><p>Receiver Luther Burden, who was concussed late in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>' win against the Buccaneers, has cleared protocol, coach Ben Johnson said. That puts him in line to play Sunday against the Saints. </p><p>Burden took a hit to the helmet from Bucs linebacker Reuben Bain and fumbled the ball in the fourth quarter. He practiced Monday, but that wasn't a guarantee that he had cleared protocol.</p><p>The second-year player leads the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/11/17/how-jacksonville-jaguars-chicago-bears-week-13-nfl-flex-flexible-scheduling-fox-cbs-nbc-roger-goodell" target="_blank" >Bears</a> with 644 receiving yards this season. His four receiving touchdowns are twice as many as Colston Loveland, who is second on the team. </p><h3><b>Gordon hurt</b></h3><p>Slot cornerback Kyler Gordon hurt his shoulder against the Buccaneers, Johnson said. The team isn't treating his injury as something major, though he didn't practice Monday. Gordon left the game but returned, and the team did not report the exact nature of his injury.</p><p>"We'll see as the week goes along ..." Johnson said. "It's more a day-by-day thing for us right now."</p><p>Gordon is second on the team with four sacks.</p><h3><b>Fines</b></h3><p>Rookie receiver Zavion Thomas was fined $6,901 for striking Bucs cornerback Jacob Parrish in the facemask, which drew a 15-yard penalty. Defensive end Austin Booker was fined $6,457 for illegal use of helmet.</p>

entries.title: White Sox second baseman Chase Meidroth wins AL Silver Slugger award
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> hitting coach Derek Shomon believes second baseman Chase Meidroth is still a work in progress, only scratching the surface of his overall ability.</p><p>“Chase can win a batting title,” Shomon told the Sun-Times in late September.</p><p>For now, how about a Silver Slugger?</p><p>The 25-year-old Meidroth was honored with the award for the American League’s best offensive player at his position after hitting .276/.350/.415 this season with a career-high 16 home runs. His 90 runs scored ranked 11th in the AL. Meidroth is the first second baseman in White Sox history to win a Silver Slugger Award.</p><p>A diminutive contact hitter lacking standout raw power and speed, Meidroth was once seen as the third piece of the four-player return the White Sox acquired from the Red Sox in exchange for Garrett Crochet after the 2024 season. Upon arrival in the organization, many within the White Sox thought by the time the team reached contention, he would be a superb utility player. Instead, Meidroth has blossomed into arguably the best all-around second baseman in the AL during his second major-league season.</p><p>Meidroth led all AL second baseman in wins above replacement in 2026, was one of three finalists for the Gold Glove award at second for his defense, and now has edged out Kody Clemens of the Twins for the top offensive honor at the position. After never so much as reaching double-digit home runs in any of his seasons in the minor leagues, Meidroth’s 16 homers were an easy career-high, and that total doesn’t include his cathartic three-run blast that effectively sealed the Sox’ Wild Card series victory in Houston; their first playoff series win in 21 years.</p><p>“When he does hit balls 95-plus mph, he’s hitting them at way better angles this year than last year,” said Shomon, explaining how Meidroth’s vaulted his production without a physical transformation. “After he hit his first five or six, Joel [McKeithan] and I were like ‘Dude, he can probably hit 15 or 20 this year.’ If you ask Chase — I think Chase can hit 20 every year.”</p><p>It’s good to have next year’s goal already set.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Mayor Johnson says Ashlee Gabrysch, his third CFO in the last year, 'wasn't a good fit'
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson on Tuesday defended the behind-the-scenes maneuvering that triggered the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/13/ashlee-gabrysch-chief-financial-officer-resigns-chicago-mayor-brandon-johnson" >resignation of Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch</a>, saying she “wasn’t a good fit” and that he doesn’t always “get it right” when it comes to making personnel decisions.</p><p>“I wish her well,” Johnson said of Gabrysch, his third CFO in a year.</p><p>After striking that seemingly conciliatory tone, Johnson doubled down on the counteroffensive he launched against Gabrysch on her way out.</p><p>The mayor once again accused Gabrysch of violating the law when she directed the city treasurer to forward a $75 million up-front payment from the New York investment firm that acquired Chicago parking meters to the four city employee pension funds “without proper legal authority or following the required processes.”</p><p>Asked if there should be “consequences” for Gabrysch’s decision not to wait until the city clerk had published a pamphlet reflecting the vote by a veto-proof City Council majority, Johnson said, “This is not just a description. They did not have the authorization to do it.”</p><p>The mayor said he cannot “predict the outcome” of the investigation he asked Inspector General David Glockner to conduct.</p><p>But he said, “The unauthorized payment that was made — which was illegal. There is a standard that all public officials have that we have to maintain. And it’s important that the people of Chicago know that is the expectation that I have. That is the expectation that the public has from public officials. And it’s important that we all hold to that."</p><p> Gabrysch has called Johnson's attacks a "pathetic attempt" to smear her and said, "It's a conversation I’m having with my attorneys.”</p><p>Gabrysch also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/11/16/outside-audit-city-hall-finances-cfo-resignation-ashlee-gabrysch" >told the Chicago Sun-Times </a>this week that the $75 million payment from Stonepeak Partners was forwarded to the pension funds only after a veto-proof majority of the City Council authorized it, the mayor signed the ordinance, and top mayoral aides were informed the payment was being made.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Ashlee Gabrysch</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>City of Chicago via LinkedIn</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>She expressed confidence she would be vindicated by interoffice correspondence that will prove that “twenty-plus people knew this was happening,” and that the transfer she ordered was “not done behind anyone’s back.”</p><p>A former analyst for Fitch Ratings, Gabrysch resigned Friday after just three months on the job. She quit after being admonished, frozen out, and as sources closes to her said, bullied for publicly and privately contradicting the mayor’s claim that his $17.6 billion budget was 76% structurally balanced.</p><p>Gabrysch said only 56% of the moves the mayor had made to erase a $882 million shortfall were structural, because settlements tied to allegations of police abuse — and the $480 million in borrowing Johnson ordered to cover those costs — should not count as structural solutions.</p><p>On Tuesday, Johnson downplayed the conflict as a “technical” disagreement that was resolved by “providing both scenarios” in what he called the “spirit of full transparency.”</p><p>Acting CFO Michael Belsky called the disagreement “much ado about nothing,” even after Gabrysch said that, “to continue in this role would be to compromise my integrity and professional obligation.”</p><p>“The mayor found it very important for people to understand the size of this liability of settlements and judgments. It’s significant of no doing of his own. This goes back to the '80s and '90s. These were terrible acts. We have a moral obligation to pay these people out, and the courts are requiring us to do that,” Belsky said, referring to police misconduct settlements involving defendants often tortured into confessing to crimes they did not commit.</p><p>“Because you can issue bonds every year at any time to meet an obligation like settlements and judgments that have been with us for a few years, you can say that’s a structural match there … The other way to look at it is you take that out, and then you just match up revenues and expenditures. … These are the two ways the budget can be interpreted. No one was told you only have to talk about it one way.”</p><p>Johnson said he “welcomes more transparency” of city finances — including the three-year review that opposition alderpersons hope to launch Wednesday.</p><p>But his more immediate concern is passing a balanced budget that can attract the 26 votes needed for passage at a time when a group of 28 alderpersons have declared their opposition to more than $400 million of his tax-the-rich ideas.</p><p>Johnson challenged his critics to present revenue-raising alternatives to the tax increases they don't like — even though they claim the onus is on him.</p><p>"If the City Council wants more savings, they're gonna have to lay people off," he said. "I'm not gonna do that. People are hurting. That's what sucks about all this."</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams: 'I’ve moved on' from 4-interception debacle, ready for home stretch of playoff race
entries.summary: <p>This is the time for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a> to put it all together and jump fully into being the franchise quarterback.</p><p>Williams is deep into his second season in coach Ben Johnson’s offense, he’s had an extra week to rest his ailing hamstring and he’s heading into a key stretch of games for the Bears’ playoff push and the team’s evaluation of him. Elite quarterbacks rise to the moment, and the ultra-competitive NFC leaves little margin for mistakes.</p><p>That starts with Williams showing Sunday against the struggling Saints that his four-interception performance in an ugly win over the Buccaneers two weeks ago truly was an aberration rather than a step backward.</p><p>He called some of those interceptions “funky” and one a “dumb decision,” but he’s getting over it.</p><p>“I don’t want to let my teammates down ... so that’s the frustrating part that lingers,” Williams said after practice Tuesday. “But the other half of it is, I’ve thrown three picks before. In big games, I’ve thrown picks — picks that seal the game and things like that. So I’ve moved on from it.”</p><p>Williams has played six games: four beauties (Panthers, Falcons, Patriots, Seahawks), one dud (Vikings) and one total disaster (Bucs).</p><p>That totals out to a 68.7 completion percentage (third in the NFL), 257.7 yards per game (10th), eight touchdown passes (22nd), five interceptions (10th-fewest) and a 95.4 passer rating (14th). He is on track for career bests in most categories.</p><p>The Bears’ defense bailed him out against the Bucs on a night when he completed fewer than 60% of his passes, threw four interceptions, including two in scoring range, and had a 61.5 passer rating.</p><p>There are few blessings in the NFL like getting that type of wakeup call without having to take a loss. If that’s a one-off that gets Williams to refocus and return to how sharp he was in the previous three games, which was the best stretch of his career, it was perfectly timed.</p><p>After the Saints game, the Bears have a quick turnaround to visit the Lions, who lead the NFC North, on Thanksgiving. Six of their final eight games are against teams currently in the playoff field, including some Super Bowl contenders like the Bills and Jaguars.</p><p>Every game will be high-stakes from here on out, including Sunday. While the Saints are 3-6 and have one of the league’s worst defenses, the Bears simply can’t afford a slip in a race so tight that a team can slide from the top of the field to the outside of it in a blink.</p><p>“The pressure, I don't think we have that here inside the building,” Williams said. “One week we can be [perceived as] Super Bowl contenders … one week we can be the worst team in the league, and that comes from the outside.</p><p>“We know who we are. We are confident in who we are and what we're building and what we're going for. And so with that we've got to keep focusing on each week, and then that whole [pressure] idea goes away.”</p><p>While the Bears have the toughest remaining schedule in the league by opponent winning percentage, they should be up for the challenge. All the pieces should be in place, especially for Williams. It’s all been building toward this. The Bears never got to this point with their last two first-round picks at quarterback, Mitch Trubisky and Justin Fields, but now they’re in a position where if Williams takes off, there’s no ceiling on them.</p><p>Johnson would agree that Williams should be full-go.</p><p>He believes he is fully fluent in the offense, and said Tuesday the coaching staff isn’t “hindered in any way from the schematics of what we’re able to put in — the details, the alerts.” Nothing should be new or complicated to Williams anymore.</p><p>The injury doesn’t seem to be a factor, either, and Williams said he doesn’t feel as though he’s playing hurt, clarifying that when he said this would affect him all season, he meant in terms of the extra work he’s doing outside of games to maintain strength.</p><p>If it’s limiting him, Johnson hasn’t noticed.</p><p>"I just go off of what my eyes show me,” Johnson said. “I see a player that is 100%.</p><p>“I really don't call plays with that in mind. Our medical team has cleared him to go; he's given the green light to me. Everything is at our disposal right now.”</p><p>That should enable Williams to play his best and get back to what he did when he was his sharpest. In the wins over the Falcons, Patriots and Seahawks, he completed 73.8% of his passes, averaged 286.7 yards and didn’t commit a turnover.</p><p>He looked like a championship-level quarterback. Now he gets a chance to prove that’s truly what he is.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: Seiya Suzuki rejects Cubs’ qualifying offer, turning down one-year deal worth $23.15 million
entries.summary: <p>Seiya Suzuki won’t be returning to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> for a year and $23.15 million.</p><p>The outfielder rejected the team’s qualifying offer Tuesday, all but ensuring a much larger payday on the free-agent market.</p><p>Though the decision doesn’t completely close the book on Suzuki’s time on the North Side, the Cubs ensured they’ll receive a draft pick should he sign elsewhere. And given that he’s one of this winter’s top free-agent hitters and that the Cubs are focusing on pitching this offseason, that wouldn’t be a shocking outcome.</p><p>Still, the team has interest in bringing Suzuki back, if such a move fits with their other offseason plans.</p><p>“He’s a great player that would fit really well with our lineup,” general manager Carter Hawkins said last week during the GM meetings in Las Vegas. “It’s how all the different pieces of the puzzle come together toward the best team for 2027 and the future.</p><p>“He’s a great teammate, fits well into our lineup. … He’s one of the best hitters in the league. Of course, we would be silly not to have interest in reuniting with him.”</p><p>While the Cubs have plans for an internal replacement, should it come to that, in the form of utility man Matt Shaw, a Suzuki departure would blast a sizable hole in the lineup that scored more runs than any other during the 2026 regular season.</p><p>Suzuki finished with a 131 OPS-plus that made him 31% more productive than the average major league hitter, belting 26 homers and racking up 86 RBIs. He walked 81 times and reached base at a .368 clip, both single-season highs in his five years since arriving in the United States.</p><p>In addition to spending much of the campaign as the Cubs’ second best hitter behind MVP-winner Pete Crow-Armstrong, Suzuki’s significant defensive improvement made him a Gold Glove finalist in right field.</p><p>It makes for big shoes to fill as the Cubs could be stuck <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/11/cubs-free-agents-mlb-offseason-left-field-right-field-catcher-ian-happ-seiya-suzuki-carson-kelly-miguel-amaya-pedro-ramirez-matt-shaw" >attempting to replace a third of their lineup</a>, with Suzuki joined on the free-agent market by left fielder Ian Happ and catcher Carson Kelly. Infielder Pedro Ramirez could wind up stepping in for Happ, putting a pair of youngsters in the corner-outfield spots.</p><p>But the front office has made it clear it plans to focus much of its energy and resources on remaking the pitching staff this winter, with all five arms who ended the season in the starting rotation free agents and several in-house candidates to replace them coming off significant injuries.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Bears coach Ben Johnson not worried about NFC North race — yet
entries.summary: <p>Ben Johnson doesn’t care what’s happening elsewhere in the NFC North.</p><p> He’s told his players to follow suit.</p><p>"It really doesn't matter right now,” the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach said before Tuesday’s practice. “Once again, it's all about winning this week. So, we'll worry about everything else when it's time. It's not time for that.”</p><p>It won’t be for a while.</p><p>“The division, the big picture, that'll take care of itself,” Johnson said. “We're still in November, so we just need to find a way to win this week.”</p><p>The Bears play in the best division in the NFL, the NFC North, where all four teams would make the playoffs were the season to end today. The Vikings have become the NFC’s trendiest team after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nfl/2026/11/15/vikings-beat-packers-30-10-in-kirk-cousins-return-jordan-love-is-sacked-8-times" >beating the Packers on Sunday.</a> The Packers and Bears — and even the Lions, though they've since lost their two most prominent defensive players — have held that title at various points this season.</p><p>Sunday’s opponent, the Saints, decidedly do not. They’re 3-6 in an NFC South where no one has a winning record. The Bears are 11½-point favorites. To keep pace with the rest of the conference — one that includes the Seahawks, 49ers and Rams fighting for playoff spots out west — the Bears can’t afford to be complacent Sunday.</p><p>“You can’t look forward, you can’t look behind,” receiver <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/17/bears-report-luther-burden-kyler-gordon-clears-concussion-protocol-shoulder-injury-nfl" target="_blank" >Luther Burden</a> said. “You have to look at what’s here right now.”</p><p>That’s been Johnson’s message just as much as other coaching points: stopping quarterback pressure over the center and guards. sharpening the run game, improving their turnover differential and fine-tuning special teams. The Bears held a padded practice Tuesday, which helped them address those issues at full speed.</p><p>“The NFL will humble you,” cornerback Tyrique Stevenson said. “As soon as you start pushing teams off to the side and say, ‘We’re a good team — we think we can do this,’ that’s when you get humbled. He does a great job of letting us know it’s 1-0 each week.”</p><p>The Bears would have every reason to look ahead. They play Johnson’s former team, the Lions, on Thanksgiving, followed by the juggernaut Jaguars the following week at Soldier Field. After a game in Miami, the Bears go to Buffalo before playing their three division rivals — the Packers, Lions and at the Vikings — in the final three weeks of the season.</p><p>Johnson likes to split his season into four-week quarters. With eight games left to play, Johnson has segmented the third quarter of the season into games against the Saints, Lions, Jaguars and Dolphins. He and the Bears benefited from their bye being smack in the middle of the season.</p><p>“I think the bye week came at a really good time for everybody to step back and catch their breath,” Johnson said. “And now we're in it. …<br>“We took a big-picture view of what we've done well, where we need to improve and really what we need to focus on for the next four weeks.”</p><p>The division will sort itself out long after that.</p><p>“We're the best division in football …” defensive tackle Grady Jarrett said. “By the end of the season everything will take care of itself. … It's a different brand of football played up here. And it's been fun. It's going to come down to the wire. So it's exciting, and it's going to be a heavyweight match.”</p><p>But first, the Bears have to beat the Saints. The rest of their schedule won’t be nearly as relevent unless they do.</p><p>“When those times come, they're going to come,” Jarrett said. “But we've got to focus on where we're at right now and take care of the things that we're going to be able to control — and that's the next game ahead of us.”</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Need a giant cheesecake-shaped float for your parade? Chicago's Hank Fiene is your man
entries.summary: <p>Hank Fiene scrapes a wire brush across an enormous slice of cheesecake.</p><p>Or, rather, a triangular wooden frame covered in plywood, then encased in sheets of Styrofoam, which Fiene is transforming into a wedge of Eli's cherry cheesecake eight feet long and four feet tall, rotating on a circular platform on a float in the parade at the Wintrust Magnificent Mile Lights Festival this Saturday, Nov. 21. He vigorously scrubs what will be the crust.</p><p>"This float has to be done by Thursday morning," says Fiene, coated in tiny bits of polystyrene, standing in the cluttered, sprawling warehouse of ABC Parade Floats, in Ashburn on the city's Southwest Side.</p><p>"There used to be eight parade float companies in the Chicagoland area," he says. "There are only two of us left in the Midwest now. Most of the mom-and-pop companies went out of business in 2008 and COVID took the rest."</p><p>Fiene, who started ABC in 1990, supplies floats to about 70 parades a year. </p><p>"We do just about all the parades in Chicago," he said. "St. Patrick's Day. Polish Constitution. Chicago Pride. Bud Billiken, Mexican Independence, and of course the Magnificent Mile Lights Festival. And we do Seattle, New York, Nebraska, Columbus, Ohio. Wherever you might need one. I have a motto: 'If you can afford it, we can do it.'"</p><p>The Eli's float is unusual, in that it has to be built from scratch.</p><p>"The majority of the work are stock floats," said Fiene. "We just change the colors and put a name on it."</p><p>Growing up on the South Side, Fiene dreamed of being a portrait artist, then "found out you have to die before you can make any money."</p><p>So he shifted to the idea of being a commercial artist.</p><p>"But you need a lot of experience for that," he says.</p><p>So he went into the parade float business as a teenager, and still marvels at his good fortune.</p><p>"I'm always amazed I make a living doing this," he says. "C'mon, I build parade floats."</p><p>Fiene might not be the usual definition of an artist, but is not without creative pride. For a Los Angeles Persian pride parade, he crafted a cuneiform cylinder 15 feet long with historically accurate writing. He shows off a pair of grapefruit-sized artificial cherries that will go atop the cheesecake slice.</p><p>"Normally, I would have carved these myself," he says. "But I had no time." So he bought them off Amazon. He almost apologetically admits that the letters spelling out "King of Chicago Cheesecake" and portraits of Eli Schulman, founder of Eli's, were cut, not by hand, but by a CNC machine, which is computer-controlled.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a10000" name="image-a10000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/953b43c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fe9%2Ffc72cf744f49b3ed6ac36bf5db97%2Fsteinbergwednesdayfloat-2611180058.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/dd887ca/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fe9%2Ffc72cf744f49b3ed6ac36bf5db97%2Fsteinbergwednesdayfloat-2611180058.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/10def06/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fe9%2Ffc72cf744f49b3ed6ac36bf5db97%2Fsteinbergwednesdayfloat-2611180058.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Hank Fiene, owner of ABC Parade Floats, 3375 W. Columbus, works on sculpting styrofoam into a giant slice of Eli’s Cheesecake for one of 40 floats that will appear Saturday, Nov. 21 in the largest nighttime parade in the country, part of the Wintrust Magnificent Mile Lights Festival, marking its 35th year on North Michigan Avenue. on Thursday, November 16, 2026. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/10def06/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fe9%2Ffc72cf744f49b3ed6ac36bf5db97%2Fsteinbergwednesdayfloat-2611180058.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/13e65d6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fe9%2Ffc72cf744f49b3ed6ac36bf5db97%2Fsteinbergwednesdayfloat-2611180058.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/10def06/2147483647/strip/true/crop/8192x4598+0+433/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F19%2Fe9%2Ffc72cf744f49b3ed6ac36bf5db97%2Fsteinbergwednesdayfloat-2611180058.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Hank Fiene, owner of ABC Parade Floats, 3375 W. Columbus, works on sculpting a giant slice of Eli’s Cheesecake for one of 40 floats that will appear in the Wintrust Magnificent Mile Lights Festival Nov. 21. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"We love Hank. He's a character; he does great work. Everyone knows, you want a parade float, you call Hank," says Marc Schulman, Eli's son and president of Eli's Cheesecake, who has publicized his product through just about every known means of communication — including, I should point out, advertising on my blog — but this year thought he'd try marketing via parade float. </p><p>"We've never done this before," Schulman says. "We thought it would be really fun to be part of the procession."</p><p>A procession that is now the largest nighttime parade in the country, having been started by Schulman 35 years ago.</p><p>"We needed an event before the lights were lit," says Schulman. "The first year was a few carriages and double-decker buses. The street wasn't even closed. Now it's in league with Macy's and the Rose Bowl parades."</p><p>The CNC machine also constructed the bascule bridge that will go up and down on the "Choose Chicago" float. Fiene's masterpiece several years ago was a float for Garrett's popcorn that fired a fountain of popcorn into the air.</p><p>Some floats are claimed by those who commissioned them. Others are broken down for useful parts — the ABC warehouse is a cluttered jumble of giant candy canes, life-size reindeer, suns, rainbows, bells, and sturdy copper rails that get brought out for the three parades a year featuring Plumbers Union Local 130.</p><p>I mention this seems one profession so far unaffected by artificial intelligence, but Fiene corrects me.</p><p>"I get people who send sketches created by AI, and you'll get something not physically possible," he says. "Or it'll just be wrong: showing the Chicago Water Tower along the Chicago River."</p><p>The next step with the cheesecake slice is to apply a coat of Flexcoat epoxy, to protect the Styrofoam — floats get manhandled, and it won't do to have a chunk break off mid-parade. Then paint.</p><p>But first, Fiene cleans up in a manner I've never seen anyone do before: he grabs a leaf blower and directs it at himself, blasting away bits of Styrofoam.</p><p>"One thing when you build parade floats — you learn different uses for things," Fiene says.</p>

entries.title: Bears QB Caleb Williams: Pete Crow-Armstrong's MVP a celebration for Chicago sports 'friend group'
entries.summary: <p>The celebration of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong winning the National League MVP was more than just a party to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>. Beyond being a star-studded dinner at Adalina Prime, it was symbolic of the culture Williams wants to establish in Chicago sports.</p><p>“That’s one of the coolest things about being here in Chicago and what we’re building: It’s not just Chicago Bears, it’s us as Chicago athletes,” he said after practice Tuesday. “This is one of those steppingstones for Pete as his career goes, but also us as a friend group. We want to support each other, we want to show up for each other.”</p><p>Williams and Crow-Armstrong have become close friends over the past three years and often have shown up to each other’s games, as well as attending other games together. The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls" >Bulls’ </a>Caleb Wilson is part of that group, too, and former Bulls star Derrick Rose and Bears wide receiver Rome Odunze attended the MVP dinner as well.</p><p>Music video director and entrepreneur Cole Bennett, another local, directed a video commemorating Crow-Armstrong’s MVP, and when he asked Williams to star in it, Williams immediately responded, “Of course.”</p><p>Williams’ and Crow-Armstrong’s careers have both been on the rise, and Crow-Armstrong set the pace by breaking out as an All-Star in 2025 and becoming the talk of the city. Williams then put his stamp on the sports skyline with late-game heroics and the Bears’ first playoff win in 15 years.</p><p>This season, as Crow-Armstrong ran ahead of the field for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/11/12/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-nl-mvp-award-gold-glove-platinum-glove-home-runs-stolen-bases-40-40-season" >National League MVP, </a>which he won unanimously, Williams vaulted himself into MVP contention as well with a brilliant three-game stretch coming off his hamstring injury.</p><p>The biggest thing Williams has gotten from watching Crow-Armstrong play is the way he ignites the crowd and his teammates with his enthusiasm.</p><p>“Pete always brings that energy,” Williams said “He’s such a nice guy, but when he gets on the field he turns into a little rocket. ... He always has good energy around him and about him, so that’s special about him.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/12/bears-caleb-williams-pete-crow-armstrong-stars-national-league-mvp-video-nfl" >Bears QB Caleb Williams stars in Cubs’ PCA MVP video</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/11/bears-qb-caleb-williams-celebrates-platinum-glove-with-pete-crow-armstrong" >Bears QB Caleb Williams celebrates platinum glove with Pete Crow-Armstrong</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Actors with Chicago ties among winners at Critics Choice's Celebration of Black Cinema & Television
entries.summary: <p>This year’s awardees at the Critics Choice Association’s ninth annual Celebration of Black Cinema & Television Monday paid tribute to Black artists, including several with Chicago connections. And whenever we talk about Hollywood, just like the song “(Get Your Kicks on) Route 66” says, the road “winds from Chicago to L.A., more than two thousand miles all the way.”</p><p>Honorees included homegrown talent, actors who came to the Windy City to hone their craft and those who are simply portraying some of the Chicago area’s icons.</p><p>Roy Wood Jr. began the show by remarking how there is still cause for Black people to celebrate despite the attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure
