Bernie Mac and Adele Givens.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Leon Bennett/Getty Images for Critics Choice Association</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>While he didn’t grow up in Chicago, he does have a family connection.</p><p>“My pops [Roy Wood Sr.] is old-school Chicago, WVON [radio station] and one of the founding members of the National Black Network. Chicago has always been a centerpiece of Black excellence and Black entertainment. It’s the only city that gave us both a king and a queen of comedy. Bernie Mac and Adele Givens. And Adele Givens, that’s my comedy mom, man.”</p><p>Wood was not the only funny person to have a Chicago connection at Monday’s event. Emmy Award winner Lamorne Morris received the Comedy Award for his work as Robbie Robertson in Prime Video’s superhero series “Spider-Noir.” Morris grew up on the South Side and attended high school in Glen Ellyn. He also cut his teeth at the famed Second City.</p><p>His acceptance speech put all other comics on notice as he pointed out all the legendary comedians in the house, from Chris Rock and Eddie Murphy to Quinta Brunson and Tommy Davidson, but noted that he was the one being acknowledged in the comedy category. Backstage, he was a bit more humble and thanked one of his teachers.</p><p>“Mr. Dobez, I remember, would always give me time in class to say something. He’s like, ‘Get it off your chest. Say what you gotta say.’”</p><p>And of his Second City training, he said, “It just taught me to stay quick, to just always be listening. Listening to what your scene partner is saying and how they feel, reading body language. Second City teaches you all of that.”</p><p> He also gave a shoutout to his church family, Colonial Village Church of Christ in West Pullman, remarking how whenever he’s in town, that is one of his first stops. However, while his mom, Gwenett Morris, did give him praise for his accomplishments, she also let it be known that his religious foundation comes with some expectations.</p><p>“He’s been through a lot. Some doors have been closed, but he never gave up,” she said. “The only thing I don’t like is the profanity.” </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-6d0000" name="image-6d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/8e9834c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3744x2101+0+197/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F11%2F7e%2F3ef1ea394671a8e07d78af12437e%2F2305477413.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/bb2aa70/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3744x2101+0+197/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F11%2F7e%2F3ef1ea394671a8e07d78af12437e%2F2305477413.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fd955cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3744x2101+0+197/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F11%2F7e%2F3ef1ea394671a8e07d78af12437e%2F2305477413.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Lamorne Morris speaks onstage during The Critics Choice Association's 9th Annual Celebration of Black Cinema & Television at Fairmont Century Plaza on November 16, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fd955cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3744x2101+0+197/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F11%2F7e%2F3ef1ea394671a8e07d78af12437e%2F2305477413.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/82b82a9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3744x2101+0+197/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F11%2F7e%2F3ef1ea394671a8e07d78af12437e%2F2305477413.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fd955cb/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3744x2101+0+197/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F11%2F7e%2F3ef1ea394671a8e07d78af12437e%2F2305477413.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Lamorne Morris accepts the Comedy Award for his work as Robbie Robertson in Prime Video’s superhero series “Spider-Noir.” He grew up on the South Side and attended high school in Glen Ellyn. He also cut his teeth at the famed Second City.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Leon Bennett/Getty Images for Critics Choice Association</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Fellow Second City alum Brunson received the Groundbreaker Award for creating, executive producing and starring in ABC’s “Abbott Elementary.”</p><p>Brunson had difficulty reading the teleprompter, which prompted laughs from the audience, and she just leaned in like an improv professional. She said she usually does not write her speeches, but this award was especially important to her, so she wrote one. And she exclaimed that she was going to read it, which drew laughs, cheers and applause from the audience.</p><p>Pulitzer Prize winner Katori Hall was honored with the Showrunner Award for Starz’s “P-Valley” and was grateful that her play “Hoodoo Love” made it all the way to Chicago and played at such venues as the Athenaeum Center for Thought and Culture.</p><p>“It was my first celebration of the African American vernacular and this beautiful celebration of the Black American South.”</p><p>Hall described Chicago as “Up South,” referencing the migration from the South. She was visibly grateful for her work’s reach and impact.</p><p>“I’m seeing how my work is going to places that it needs to be. Where my family is, where my framily [friends and family] is. And so just really, really proud of that connection.”</p><p>Jaalen Best was honored with the Rising Star Award for his performance as Cassius Clay in Prime Video’s series “The Greatest.” The series highlights Ali’s life in Chicago, and Best remarked on how Chicago residents helped him understand Ali better.</p><p>“That’s where I got an idea of how much he meant, and how much he could transcend a place and bring people together in different ways.”</p><p>And on visiting Chicago for the first time and only experiencing Downtown, Best recalled turning to his co-star and Chicagoan Kai Parham, who plays Rudy, Ali’s brother.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f70000" He’s like, ‘You ain’t even seen nothing yet.’”</p><p>Parham, present to support Best, added, “Being able to see and meet him at ground zero in the audition process, to now being able to see this moment, it’s so well-deserved.”</p><p> Each honoree paid tribute to Debbie Allen, who received the Icon Award. Allen was being celebrated for her outstanding work as a choreographer, director, actor, producer and advocate as well as for opening doors. In her acceptance speech, she defined icon: “What is an icon to me? Someone, an artist or a leader at the top of their field, not just great at what they do but someone who has an impact and influence in the community. Someone who is breaking down barriers. Someone who is creating opportunities and making the word possibility accessible to all of us.”</p><p>The celebration was clearly about the accomplishments but also about possibilities, and Allen’s presence capped off a night where excellence was celebrated and the community was elevated.</p><p>“You have chosen to recognize me. That you see me. I’m not one really looking to be seen because I’m so busy doing what I do,” Allen said. </p><p>But don’t think the celebration ended when the curtains closed. The joy and community extended to the afterparty and beyond. To see that, you would have needed to travel “more than two thousand miles all the way.”</p><p>And if you didn’t, you can watch the entire show on the <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/c/CriticsChoice" target="_blank" >Critics Choice YouTube channel</a> on Dec. 15.</p>

entries.title: David Byrne-backed ‘Theater of the Mind’ to end Chicago run in January
entries.summary: <p>The Goodman Theatre has announced that after 5,000 performances, the David Byrne-backed <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/02/05/david-byrne-chicago-theater-of-the-mind-goodman-talking-heads" target="_blank" ><u>“Theater of the Mind”</u></a> will close in January.</p><p>The fully immersive show opened in March as an experimental addition to the company’s 100th season. The production, located in the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2025/10/28/david-byrne-chicago-goodman-theatre-immersive-theater-of-the-mind" target="_blank" ><u>Reid Murdoch building</u></a> downtown, received mostly <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/03/27/review-theater-of-the-mind-david-byrne-goodman-theatre" target="_blank" ><u>positive reviews</u></a>. (I wrote <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/03/27/review-theater-of-the-mind-david-byrne-goodman-theatre" target="_blank" ><u>in March</u></a> that the show “exists somewhere in the margins of creepy festival funhouse meets cool high school science experiment. It’s trippy. It’s unique. And somewhere buried in the cool head tricks there is a story about revisiting the pivotal moments of our lives and questioning if we can trust our own recollections.”)</p><p>An ambitious project created by Byrne and Mala Gaonkar, “Theater of the Mind” takes audiences on a journey through their own memories. Directed by immersive theater aficionado Andrew Scoville, the production features lifelike sets, hands-on experiments and a tour guide, named David, clad in the fashion of a childhood David Byrne.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ec0000" name="image-ec0000"></a> <picture being passive observers and having the story kind of wash over them,” Scoville said during a preview show just before opening last spring. “More and more people want to step inside the story.”</p><p>The production utilized 19,000 square-feet of space to drive home the desired feeling of audiences being transported into another reality. The 75-minute journey challenged viewers' senses — including a cool experiment with taste — and allowed audience members to dance with their David.</p><p>Nearly 50,000 people have seen the show, the Goodman said this week. In a joint statement, co-creators Byrne and Gaonkar said, “Audiences here were so curious and open to a new theatrical experience showing how loose our hold is on our seemingly strongest memories… We are forever grateful that our show enjoyed such a lengthy run in this open-hearted community.”</p><p>“Theater of the Mind” will continue through the holidays and stage the final show on Jan. 27, 2027</p>

entries.title: White Sox select contracts of prospects William Bergolla Jr. and Jaden Woods, DFA Joey Bart
entries.summary: <p>When Major League Baseball last faced a lockout in 2021, negotiations over a new collective bargaining agreement stretched into March, canceling December’s annual winter meetings and Rule 5 Draft.</p><p>While history seems primed to repeat itself, teams have been instructed to conduct business as usual. So with Nov. 17 representing the deadline for clubs to protect Rule 5-eligible prospects by adding them to the 40-man roster, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> are bestowing such honors upon infielder William Bergolla Jr. and left-handed reliever Jaden Woods, both of whom finished this past season at the Triple-A level.</p><p>In a corresponding move, veteran backup catcher Joey Bart was designated for assignment to make room on the team’s full 40-man roster. When <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/11/17/white-sox-add-to-starting-rotation-by-signing-free-agent-right-hander-dustin-may" >Dustin May’s three-year, $52.5 million deal </a>becomes official later this week, the White Sox will need to make another corresponding move. An arbitration-eligible Jordan Leasure, already set to miss the entire 2027 season while recovering from elbow surgery, is an early place to look.</p><p>The headliner is Bergolla, a slick-fielding 22-year-old middle infielder whose crisp footwork allows him to cover shortstop despite a diminutive frame and the lack of a big throwing arm. Acquired from the Phillies for reliever Tanner Banks, Bergolla had the lowest strikeout rate for any minor league hitter at a full-season affiliate in 2025, coupled with bottom-of-the-scale raw power. His efforts to add strength and bat speed were on display early last year, and he seemed primed to make his major-league debut when he hit .457/.525/.571 in his first 10 games at Triple-A in 2026.</p><p>Instead, Bergolla was sidelined for over three months with a right shin bruise after an outfield collision with Sam Antonacci, and suffered a season-ending right fibular fracture in July during his first rehab game. Bergolla recently completed a running progression as part of his injury recovery and general manager Chris Getz name-dropped him last week in Las Vega as a likely 2027 contributor. </p><p>With the Sox not heavily prioritizing outside additions to reload their bullpen, the 24-year-old Woods could easily find himself in Chicago next year as well. Woods was acquired from Pittsburgh last July alongside the 34th overall pick in the draft (which became Landon Thome) in exchange for Jacob Gonzalez and Brandon Eisert. Possessing a mid-90s fastball and above-average slider thrown from a low-slot release that Sox officials feel adds deception, Woods struck out 35 batters in 24 ⅓ innings at Triple-A Charlotte after the trade, and posted a 2.96 ERA.</p><p>While Bart is the corresponding move here, the 29-year-old veteran likely wasn’t going to last the week in either regard. Acquired in August to fill the Sox’ need for a backup catcher, Bart’s season ended in just his third game with his new team when a wayward pitch fractured the fifth metacarpal in his left hand. With MLB Trade Rumors estimating that Bart was due $2.9 million in salary arbitration, he was likely to be non-tendered on Friday’s deadline for such decisions.</p><p>The Sox have already indicated they intend to add a new backup catcher this winter to play behind starter Kyle Teel.</p>

entries.title: Bally's announces $560 million loan to help bring construction of a permanent casino to the finish line
entries.summary: <p>Bally's has secured another loan to help complete its River West casino complex. </p><p>The company, which has already taken on considerable debt to complete the project, issued a statement Tuesday announcing it secured an additional $560 million loan to "repay certain outstanding indebtedness as well as for general corporate purposes."</p><p>In August, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/09/ballys-to-stop-work-on-some-amenities-at-permanent-chicago-casino-development-amid-video-gambling-dispute" target="_blank" >Bally’s paused construction</a> on the casino amid an ongoing dispute over the expansion of video gambling terminals in the city. That same month, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2026/08/17/ballys-chicago-casino-video-gambling-going-concern" target="_blank" >the company also acknowledged</a> its massive debt creates “substantial doubt about its ability to continue” over the next year. </p><p>Bally's already is on the hook for about $400 million in costs over the next two years to complete its permanent complex at 777 W. Chicago Ave. Meanwhile, the company has not been breaking even at its temporary casino at the historic Medinah Temple, 600 N. entries.title: Ethanol plant trainee charged in connection with bomb at Peoria facility
entries.summary: <p>An Illinois man who worked as a trainee at a Peoria ethanol plant was charged Tuesday by a federal grand jury with two felonies related to a bomb that was found at the facility, resulting in a mass evacuation.</p><p>Police said they found a bomb on Friday at the BioUrja facility and “rendered it safe” before allowing residents who had been evacuated to return on Saturday. About 2,500 homes within a 1-mile radius of the industrial site were evacuated, law enforcement officials said.</p><p>Andrew Kozak, 41, of Chillicothe, Illinois, was charged by the grand jury in federal court with making threats involving explosives, a felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison. He was also charged with making that threat to BioUrja Renewables over email, a felony punishable by up to five years in prison.</p><p>Kozak has been a trainee at the facility for 10 months, according to his LinkedIn page.</p><p>“Learning how to operate an ethanol plant,” Kozak wrote under his job description.</p><p>Police said the suspect was arrested at the BioUrja facility on Monday morning. They did not name Kozak at the time of his arrest.</p><p>No attorney was listed for Kozak on the federal court website. He was scheduled to make his initial appearance in federal court in Peoria on Tuesday afternoon.</p><p>The criminal complaint detailing the charges against Kozak was sealed. Law enforcement officials declined to discuss details of the case at a Tuesday news conference where they praised efforts to evacuate the area quickly on Friday night.</p><p>“While law enforcement regularly responds to bomb threats, most are deemed not credible,” said Ryan Prelsey, the special agent in charge of the FBI office in Springfield, Illinois. “But in this instance, it was. Had it not been for the swift action of the responders and the bomb technicians, this incident could have had a very different outcome.”</p><p>Kozak has a criminal record in Nebraska, where prison records show he served two years on burglary charges in three counties. He was released in 2008. Kozak went back to prison in 2013 on a burglary charge in a fourth county and was released in 2014, records show.</p><p>The BioUrja plant contains ethanol and “other highly combustible types of chemicals,” Peoria Mayor Rita Ali told WMBD-TV on Friday.</p><p></p>

entries.title: Former Chicago-area Mormon leader is sentenced to 45 years in prison in child sex abuse case in Ohio
entries.summary: <p>A child sex abuse case involving ex-Mormon figure Wade Christofferson has been playing out in the federal courthouse in Columbus, Ohio. <br>Some of the abuse Christofferson was accused of occurred in Utah.</p><p>But the Chicago area was central to the storyline involving Christofferson, who was sentenced Tuesday to 45 years in prison following his July guilty plea to coercion and enticement of a minor in a prosecution that found he molested two young children last year.</p><p>Christofferson used to live in the far northwest suburbs where he was a member and leader of a Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints congregation in Crystal Lake — and where he’s suspected of molesting children in the 1980s and 1990s.</p><p>Church leaders knew about at least some of his ugly history back then. They excommunicated him in the 1990s over child sex abuse allegations in the Chicago area, according to interviews.</p><p>But they didn’t tell the congregation — and they eventually restored him to full membership in the faith system.</p><p>When Christofferson and his family moved from the Chicago area to the Columbus area around that time, his new congregation was apparently not told about his predatory behavior either. And he had at least some access to children during that time, records show.</p><p>Christofferson’s case attracted attention in large part because he’s a brother of Mormon apostle D. Todd Christofferson, one of the top leaders of the Utah-based faith.</p><p>D. Todd Christofferson has acknowledged learning “around 2020” that Wade Christofferson had allegedly molested children years earlier.</p><p>A church spokesman said earlier this year: “While he and other family members were told of Wade’s . . . excommunication, he was not informed of the specific reasons and had no reason to suspect it was for abuse.”</p><p>“It was not until around 2020 that President Christofferson first learned of — through family disclosure — some of his brother’s history of abuse from thirty years earlier; he respected the adult victims’ wishes not to involve law enforcement at that time.”</p><p>D. Todd Christofferson has not addressed questions about whether this inaction put other kids at risk of abuse.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-720000" name="image-720000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/74d52cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe7%2F06%2Fc08ae3864fabbd71cbaf1ef34a92%2Flds.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/33f8485/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe7%2F06%2Fc08ae3864fabbd71cbaf1ef34a92%2Flds.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7791b6d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe7%2F06%2Fc08ae3864fabbd71cbaf1ef34a92%2Flds.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Mormon church leader D. Todd Christofferson." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7791b6d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe7%2F06%2Fc08ae3864fabbd71cbaf1ef34a92%2Flds.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/69b30c2/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe7%2F06%2Fc08ae3864fabbd71cbaf1ef34a92%2Flds.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7791b6d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2100x1179+0+111/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe7%2F06%2Fc08ae3864fabbd71cbaf1ef34a92%2Flds.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Mormon church leader D. Todd Christofferson.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>He couldn’t immediately be reached for comment.</p><p>While Tuesday’s sentencing is a bookend to the criminal case, it doesn’t end the saga. Numerous questions remain about who in church leadership may have covered for Wade Christofferson, and why.</p><p>At one point Wade Christofferson had a notation on his membership rolls signifying his abusive past, according to the church watchdog group Floodlit. But that was somehow removed — and experts say it could only have been done by, or with the approval of, the faith system’s Utah-based leaders.</p><p>The Mormon church has contended with numerous sex abuse accusations in recent years and allegations of secrecy and protecting assailants over victims.</p><p>At age 73, Wade Christofferson’s prison term may translate into a life sentence, even though he could qualify for a significant break in time served if he’s not troublesome while incarcerated and takes certain classes in prison.</p><p>While in front of U.S. District Judge Edmund A. Sargus, Jr., Tuesday, he faced at least 10 years in prison, up to life.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/11/15/wade-christofferson-child-sexual-abuse-latter-day-saints-mormon-church-crystal-lake-d-todd-christofferson-brother" target="_blank" >Wife of child-molesting ex-Mormon figure once based in Chicago area calls him ‘caring,’ ‘a wonderful father’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Prosecutors said Wade Christofferson “committed hands-on sexual abuse” of a child in Utah as well as a second child in Ohio “approximately 20 times.”</p><p>He was arrested last November, and the publicity over the allegations unleashed a torrent of other accusations from the public.</p><p>Wade Christofferson’s legal team has asked that he serve his sentence close to Utah, as he has family there, including his wife Rebecca who recently sold the family home in Dublin, Ohio, and moved to the West, court records show.</p><p>But it wasn’t immediately clear where Wade Christofferson will serve his time.</p><p>The U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Ohio, Dominick S. Gerace II, said in a written statement:</p><p>“The evidence in this case demonstrates that the offenses charged were not isolated acts, but rather, that Christofferson had a longstanding sexual interest in children that spanned decades.”</p><p>“The defendant repeatedly exploited relationships of trust to gain access to vulnerable victims, inflicting lifelong harm to generations of victims and their families. The gravity of Christofferson’s crimes justifies the 45-year sentence he received today.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/09/wade-christofferson-brother-todd-latter-day-saints-mormons-child-sex-abuse" target="_blank" >Former Chicago-area Mormon figure pleads guilty to child sex crime, could face life in prison</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/05/mormon-church-child-sex-abuse-cover-up-crystal-lake-latter-day-saints-congregation-wade-christofferson" target="_blank" >Questions cloud Mormon church handling of suburban congregation’s ex-leader accused of abusing minors</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/03/30/mormon-apostle-d-todd-christofferson-latter-day-saints-wade-christofferson-child-sexual-abuse-church" target="_blank" >Top Mormon leader D.
